title: NYC Local Law 144 bias audits: what the law requires, how impact ratios work and why enforcement lags
seoTitle: NYC Local Law 144 Bias Audits Explained
description: A plain English explainer on NYC Local Law 144: which hiring tools need a bias audit, how selection rates and impact ratios are calculated, what must be posted and disclosed, and what the 2025 state audit found about enforcement.
short: NYC Local Law 144 requires employers using an automated employment decision tool on New York City candidates to have it bias audited every year, post a summary of the results and give 10 business days notice. The audit reports selection or scoring rates and impact ratios by sex, race or ethnicity and their intersections.
body:
New York City Local Law 144 bars employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool, or AEDT, on candidates or employees in the city unless the tool has had a bias audit in the past year, a summary of that audit is public, and people are told in advance that the tool will be used. The audit is a numbers exercise: it compares how often the tool selects or scores highly people of each sex, each race or ethnicity, and each intersection of the two.

What counts as an automated employment decision tool?

The law covers software derived from machine learning, statistical modelling, data analytics or AI that produces a score, classification or recommendation used to substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions about hiring or promotion. A résumé ranker that decides who a recruiter reads first can qualify. A tool that only schedules interviews or stores applications usually does not, because it is not making the judgment. The test is how the output is used, so the same product can be in scope at one employer and outside it at another. For background on how screening software scores applicants, see our explainer on ATS résumé parsing and AI screening.

Who has to commission the audit?

The employer or employment agency using the tool carries the duty, not the vendor. In practice many vendors pay for an audit of their model and share it with customers, and the city's rules allow an employer to rely on an audit that uses historical data from several employers. The audit must be done by an independent auditor, meaning a person or firm with no financial interest in the vendor or the employer and no role in building or using the tool.

How is the impact ratio calculated?

For a tool that selects people, the auditor computes a selection rate for each category: the share of candidates in that category the tool moved forward. Each rate is then divided by the rate of the most selected category. For a tool that scores people, the auditor uses a scoring rate, the share of each category scoring above the sample median, and divides in the same way.

CategoryApplicantsAdvanced by the toolSelection rateImpact ratio
Category A40012030%1.00
Category B2506024%0.80
Category C1502718%0.60

In this illustrative example, Category C advances at 60% of the rate of Category A. Local Law 144 does not set a pass mark and does not ban a tool with a low ratio; it requires the number to be calculated and published. The federal four fifths guideline, covered in our AI bias in hiring explainer, is where the 0.80 line many employers use comes from. Categories with very small samples may be left out of the calculation, but the audit has to say so and give their counts.

What has to be published and disclosed?

A summary of the most recent audit, including the date it was done, the source of the data and the impact ratios, must be posted on the employment section of the employer's website along with the date the tool was first used. Candidates and employees who live in the city must receive notice at least 10 business days before the tool is used, along with the job qualifications and characteristics the tool will assess, and information on how to request an alternative process or accommodation if one is offered. Audits expire after one year, so an annual calendar reminder is the simplest control.

How is the law enforced, and how well?

The city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection enforces the law, which was enacted in 2021, took effect on 1 January 2023 and has been enforced since 5 July 2023. Civil penalties start at $500 for a first violation and rise to as much as $1,500 for later ones, with each day of use and each missed notice counted separately.

Enforcement has been light. A December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller, covering July 2023 to June 2025, found the department received only two complaints about automated hiring tools in that period. Of 12 test calls the auditors placed to the city's 311 line, 9 were not routed correctly. The department reviewed 32 companies and found one likely violation; the state auditors looked at the same companies and found at least 17 instances of potential non compliance. The Comptroller made 13 recommendations, and according to a February 2026 summary by DCI Consulting, the department agreed to adopt most of them.

Researchers found the same gap from the employer side. A Cornell led study presented at the ACM FAccT conference in 2024, titled "Null Compliance," examined 391 employers and found just 18 posted bias audits and 13 posted transparency notices. Because the law lets employers decide for themselves whether their tool is in scope, most simply did not publish anything.

What should an employer do in 2026?

Inventory every tool that scores, ranks or filters candidates, including AI features switched on inside an existing ATS. For each one, record how its output is used and decide in writing whether it substantially assists the decision. For tools in scope, get the current audit and its date, confirm the posted summary matches it, and check that notices go out on time. With the state auditors pushing for proactive enforcement, a documented scoping decision is the cheapest defense you can have.

New York City is no longer the only rulebook. Employers hiring in several states should read Local Law 144 alongside the Colorado AI Act and the EU AI Act, and our guide chapter on bias, regulation and candidate rights compares them.

faq.q: Does Local Law 144 apply to employers outside New York City?
faq.a: It applies when the tool is used to assess candidates or employees for jobs located in New York City, or for remote roles tied to a city office, so an employer headquartered elsewhere can still be covered.

faq.q: Does a bias audit have to show the tool is fair?
faq.a: No. The law requires the impact ratios to be calculated and published, not to meet a threshold. Federal anti discrimination law still applies to the outcomes, so a low ratio is a legal risk even if the audit is filed.

faq.q: How often is a bias audit required?
faq.a: Every year. An employer can rely on an audit for one year from the date it was done, so the summary must be refreshed annually for as long as the tool is in use.

faq.q: Can the software vendor do the audit?
faq.a: No. The vendor can pay for it, but the auditor must have no financial interest in the vendor or employer and no involvement in developing or using the tool.

faq.q: What are the penalties for violating Local Law 144?
faq.a: $500 for a first violation and up to $1,500 for each later one, with each day a tool is used without an audit and each missed notice treated as a separate violation.

title: AI screening for hourly jobs: how text, chat and voice screens work and where they fail
seoTitle: AI Screening for Hourly Jobs Explained
description: How AI screening works for hourly and frontline jobs: what text, chat and voice screens check, the evidence from a 70,000 applicant field experiment, the common failure points (strict knockouts, accessibility, bias, fraud) and how to pilot it.
short: AI screening for hourly jobs uses a text, chat or voice assistant to check shift availability, location, required certifications and pay expectations, answer applicant questions and book interviews within minutes of an application. It works best when knockout questions are kept to true requirements and a manager reviews every decision.
body:
Picture a grocery chain opening a new store in six weeks. It needs 120 cashiers, stockers and deli staff, and 2,000 people apply through a text message link. Nobody in HR can phone 2,000 people, so the first conversation each applicant has is with software. That is AI screening for hourly jobs: automated, usually conversational checks that confirm the basics, answer questions and book the interview, so a manager only meets people who can actually work the shifts.

What AI screening means for hourly roles

Screening for salaried jobs is mostly about reading resumes. Hourly applicants often do not have one, apply from a phone and decide within a day or two whether to take another offer. So hourly screening focuses on a short list of facts: availability by shift, distance to the location, age or work authorization where the law requires it, required certifications such as a food handler card or forklift license, and pay expectations. The AI part is the interface. Instead of a long form, the applicant answers in a text conversation, a chat widget or a short voice call, and the system follows up when an answer is unclear.

The three formats you will see

Text and chat assistants. The applicant taps a link and a chat assistant asks a few questions, answers questions about the job and offers interview slots. Paradox built its Conversational ATS around this model, describing it as mobile first automation for frontline workers and managers. Our explainer on AI recruiting assistants covers the chat format in more depth.

Voice interviews. A voice agent calls the applicant or takes an inbound call and runs a structured interview. Fountain's Anna is pitched this way: it runs the interviews, scores applicants the same way and hands back a ranked shortlist. Fountain reports results from its own customers, such as 55 recruiter hours saved in the first month, which are vendor figures rather than independent research. See AI phone screening for how these calls work.

Screening inside an all in one platform. Some hourly HR platforms bundle screening with scheduling and payroll. Workstream lists active sourcing, applicant tracking and Voice AI next to payroll and shift scheduling, and Harri covers sourcing, application and interview management for hospitality employers. The appeal is that a new hire moves from screening to the schedule without being rekeyed.

What the evidence says

The strongest independent evidence comes from a field experiment, not a vendor deck. In Voice AI in Firms, researchers randomly assigned 70,000 applicants for customer service jobs to interviews with human recruiters or AI voice agents, with humans making the hiring decisions. Applicants interviewed by the AI were more likely to receive offers and retention was higher. Customer service is close to the hourly world, but it is still one setting, so treat the result as a reason to pilot, not proof that every format works for every role.

Where it goes wrong

Knockouts that are too strict. A rule that rejects anyone unavailable on Sunday mornings can wipe out a large share of good applicants. Review knockout questions with store managers and keep only the ones that are true requirements.

Accessibility. Text only flows can exclude people who are more comfortable speaking, and voice flows can fail applicants with hearing or speech differences. Offer a second channel and a way to reach a person.

Bias. Scoring free text or speech can encode bias, and the employer is responsible for outcomes. Track pass rates by group and read our explainer on AI bias in hiring. If any of the jobs are in New York City, a scored screen may count as an automated employment decision tool under Local Law 144.

Fake and duplicate applicants. High volume funnels attract bots and repeat applications. Some screening tools, such as Noon's inbound applicant screening, flag likely fraud alongside the fit checks; whichever tool you use, ask how it detects duplicates.

How to roll it out

Start with one role in a few locations. Write down the five or six questions a good manager would ask, decide which answers are true knockouts, and let applicants book interviews directly. Measure time from application to interview, interview show rate and 30 day retention against locations that have not switched. Keep a person on call for exceptions, and give managers a simple way to override the screen when they meet someone the rules missed.

faq.q: Does AI screening reject hourly applicants automatically?
faq.a: Many tools can end a screen when an applicant fails a knockout question, such as being unavailable for every required shift. Good setups keep those rules few and let a manager review borderline cases.

faq.q: Do hourly applicants mind being screened by AI?
faq.a: Speed matters most to hourly applicants, and a screen that books an interview the same day is usually welcome. Offering a way to reach a person and a choice of text or voice reduces drop off.

faq.q: Is AI screening legal for hourly jobs?
faq.a: Yes, but anti discrimination law applies to the outcomes, and some places add rules. New York City requires a bias audit for covered automated tools, and Colorado and the EU have their own requirements.

faq.q: What should an AI screen ask hourly candidates?
faq.a: Availability by shift, distance or commute, required licenses or certifications, start date and pay expectations, plus one or two questions about relevant experience.

title: AI in applicant tracking systems: the four jobs it does and how to judge each one
seoTitle: AI in Applicant Tracking Systems Explained
description: How AI works inside applicant tracking systems in 2026: drafting, matching and ranking, conversation and verification features from Greenhouse, iCIMS, Lever, SmartRecruiters, Ashby and Workable, where the legal risk sits and a five step way to evaluate them.
short: AI in an applicant tracking system means features built into the ATS that draft job content, match and rank applicants, hold conversations with candidates and verify that applicants are real. Ranking and screening features carry the most legal and fairness risk, so they need explanations, human review and your own before and after measurement.
body:
The short verdict: AI inside an applicant tracking system is now standard, but it does four different jobs, and a vendor that is strong at one is often average at the rest. Most of the big ATS vendors now ship some mix of drafting, matching and ranking, conversation and verification features. Knowing which of the four you are buying is the difference between a feature that saves recruiters hours and one that nobody turns on after the demo.

What AI does inside an ATS today

Drafting. The oldest use is writing: job descriptions, rejection emails and interview questions. iCIMS lists job description optimization and career site translation among its AI features, and Lever shows AI generated rejection emails alongside its screening tools. Our explainer on the AI job description generator covers this layer in depth.

Matching and ranking. This is where the stakes rise. iCIMS describes AI search and match and ranking candidates based on skills and experience. Lever shows fit scores with a written justification for each applicant. SmartRecruiters offers Winston Screen with AI driven shortlisting. Greenhouse adds talent rediscovery tools that surface qualified people already in the database and reduce duplicate applications. Some tools go further than the ATS vendors themselves: searching the candidates already stored in your ATS with the same criteria used for outbound sourcing is a separate product category that plugs into the system of record.

Conversation and coordination. Chat and voice assistants answer applicant questions, collect missing details and book interviews. SmartRecruiters says Winston Chat generates answers from your career site and knowledge base rather than a fixed script, and Greenhouse Voice AI runs a first two way voice interview on the candidate's schedule. Greenhouse Notetaker records and transcribes interviews and maps AI generated notes to scorecard questions.

Verification. The newest layer checks whether applicants are who they say they are. Greenhouse Real Talent flags suspicious applications using signals such as phone number, email, IP address and location, and lets teams block repeat spam by IP or email domain. With fake candidates on the rise, this is quickly moving from add on to requirement; see our explainer on deepfake job candidates.

From features to agents

The vocabulary shifted in 2026 from AI features to agents. Workable now markets the Workable Agent as running the top of the funnel, sourcing, screening and qualifying every candidate. iCIMS introduced agents for sourcing, matching, engagement and coordination, including a hiring agent for Microsoft Teams. Workday has folded its AI under Sana, which it says builds, orchestrates and manages agents across HR, finance and IT. The difference from a feature is that an agent takes a sequence of steps on its own, which makes the review and audit controls more important, not less.

Where the risk sits

Drafting and scheduling carry little legal risk. Ranking and screening are different, because they influence who gets an interview. In New York City, a tool that substantially assists a hiring decision can trigger the bias audit and notice rules explained in our Local Law 144 explainer, and similar rules are spreading. Vendors are responding with principles: Greenhouse says its AI can inform, summarize and surface insights but the decision stays with the employer, Ashby says its AI features can be reviewed, adjusted and switched on or off, and iCIMS points to a TRUSTe Responsible AI certification.

Those statements are a starting point, not a substitute for your own testing. A ranking model can reproduce patterns in your past hiring, as our explainer on AI bias in hiring describes, and a vendor's audit does not cover how you configure it.

How to evaluate AI in your ATS

  1. List the job each feature does. Sort the vendor's AI into drafting, ranking, conversation and verification, and decide which ones you will actually use.
  2. Ask what the model sees. Find out which fields feed a match score, whether it uses resume text only or also interview feedback, and whether you can exclude fields.
  3. Check for explanations. A score without a reason cannot be defended to a hiring manager or a regulator. Prefer tools that show why a candidate ranked where they did.
  4. Keep a human step. Make sure no candidate is rejected solely by a model, and log who made each decision.
  5. Measure before and after. Track time to first review, interview rates by group and candidate drop off for a month before switching a feature on, then compare. Vendor case studies, such as SmartRecruiters citing Frasers Group cutting time to hire from 23 to 9 days, show what is possible, not what you will get.

The ATS is still the system of record. The AI on top of it is only as useful as the data underneath and the rules you set for it, so clean, consistent stage and disposition data is the first investment to make.

faq.q: Do applicant tracking systems use AI to reject candidates?
faq.a: Many now rank or score applicants, and some screening features can end an application when a knockout question fails. Vendors such as Greenhouse say the hiring decision stays with the employer, and good practice is to keep a human review before any rejection.

faq.q: Which ATS has the best AI?
faq.a: It depends on the job you need done. Greenhouse is strong on interview notes and fraud detection, iCIMS and SmartRecruiters on matching and candidate conversation, and Lever on explained fit scores. Compare the features you will actually switch on.

faq.q: Is AI ranking in an ATS legal?
faq.a: Generally yes, but rules apply in some places. New York City's Local Law 144 requires bias audits and notices for automated employment decision tools, and the EU AI Act treats recruitment AI as high risk.

faq.q: What is the difference between an AI feature and an AI agent in an ATS?
faq.a: A feature does one task when asked, such as drafting an email. An agent carries out a sequence of steps, such as sourcing, screening and scheduling, with less prompting, so it needs stronger logging and review.

title: AI and LinkedIn InMail: what is allowed, what works and what gets accounts restricted
seoTitle: AI and LinkedIn InMail Explained
description: How AI is used with LinkedIn InMail in 2026: LinkedIn's Hiring Assistant, AI drafting you send by hand, and why automated sending tools break LinkedIn's User Agreement.
short: AI and LinkedIn InMail means using artificial intelligence to choose who to message and to write the message. LinkedIn's own Hiring Assistant and AI drafts you send by hand are within the rules; tools that automate sending on your account are not, because LinkedIn's User Agreement bans bots and unauthorized automated messaging.
body:
A recruiter opens LinkedIn Recruiter on Monday with forty passive candidates saved for a backend role and a monthly InMail allowance that will not cover them all. Artificial intelligence now shows up in three places in that workflow: inside LinkedIn's own products, in general purpose writing assistants the recruiter pastes from, and in third party tools that promise to send messages for you. Only the first two fit inside LinkedIn's rules, and that distinction decides which AI is worth paying for.

What InMail is, in one paragraph

InMail is LinkedIn's paid message to members outside your network. Recruiter, Sales Navigator and Premium plans come with a monthly allotment of credits, each message to a non connection spends one, and LinkedIn returns the credit when the person replies within 90 days. A good primer on how InMail credits and refunds work covers the mechanics; the point for AI is simple. Because unanswered messages cost money, anything that raises reply rates pays for itself, and anything that sends more low quality messages wastes credits.

AI inside LinkedIn's own products

LinkedIn now sells its flagship recruiting seat as LinkedIn Recruiter plus Hiring Assistant and describes it as agentic AI built on its member network. The Hiring Assistant 2 page splits the work into intake, sourcing, applicant evaluation, and prescreening and outreach, and says the assistant asks questions to build a sourcing strategy for the role rather than relying on keywords and filters alone. In practice that means AI that drafts and personalizes InMail from the candidate's profile, suggests who to contact next and handles parts of the follow up, all inside the product that owns the credits.

The advantage is compliance and context: the model sees the same profile data you do and works under LinkedIn's terms. The cost is that it is sold as an add on, so it raises the price of a seat that is already the most expensive line in many recruiting budgets.

AI writing assistants you copy from

Many recruiters draft InMail in a general chatbot, then paste the result into LinkedIn and send it by hand. That is allowed, because a person is still sending each message. It works best when you feed the model specifics the candidate will recognize, such as a project, a stack or a career move, and ask for something short. It works worst when the prompt is just a job title, which produces the polite, interchangeable notes candidates already ignore.

  • Give the model two facts from the profile and one honest reason the role fits.
  • Ask for under 100 words and one clear question.
  • Read every draft before sending; a wrong detail is worse than no detail.

Third party tools that automate sending

This is where the risk sits. LinkedIn's User Agreement says members may not use bots or other unauthorized automated methods to access the services, add or download contacts, or send or redirect messages, and it separately bans software, scripts, crawlers and browser plugins that scrape profiles. A browser extension that clicks send on hundreds of InMails is exactly what those clauses describe, and the account that gets restricted is the recruiter's, not the vendor's.

Teams that want automation at scale usually move it off LinkedIn instead: they find the candidate's email address or phone number and run sequences through their own email and texting tools, where they control sending limits and opt outs. Our explainer on AI recruiting assistants covers that category, and AI and candidate experience covers how candidates react to automated messages on any channel.

How to judge an AI InMail feature

QuestionGood answerRed flag
Who presses send?You, or LinkedIn's own productAn extension acting on your session
What does the draft use?Specific profile details and the roleOnly the job title
How is success measured?Replies and credit refunds per messageMessages sent per day
What happens to credits?Fewer, better targeted InMailsThe allowance runs out mid month

The honest summary: AI makes InMail better when it helps you write fewer, sharper messages, and it makes things worse when it is used to send more of them. Use LinkedIn's own assistant if the budget allows, use a writing assistant with care if it does not, and treat any tool that automates sending on your account as a liability. For how recruiters are using these tools more broadly, see AI recruitment statistics.

faq.q: Can I use ChatGPT or another chatbot to write LinkedIn InMail?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you review the draft and send it yourself. The restriction in LinkedIn's User Agreement is on bots and unauthorized automated methods that send messages, not on where the words came from.

faq.q: Does LinkedIn have its own AI for InMail?
faq.a: LinkedIn sells Hiring Assistant as an add on to LinkedIn Recruiter. Its product page describes help with intake, sourcing, applicant evaluation, prescreening and outreach.

faq.q: Is it safe to use a browser extension that sends InMail automatically?
faq.a: It is risky. LinkedIn's User Agreement prohibits software, scripts and browser plugins that scrape the service and bans bots that send messages, so the recruiter's account can be restricted.

title: AI background checks: what the software does, what the law still requires and what to ask vendors
seoTitle: AI Background Checks Explained
description: How AI is used in employment background checks in 2026: identity verification, record matching and automated adjudication, plus the FCRA and fair chance steps that still need a person.
short: An AI background check is a standard employment screening report in which software reads, matches and sorts records and applies the employer's written criteria. It speeds up routine reports, but the FCRA disclosure, authorization and adverse action steps, and any individualized review required by fair chance laws, still sit with the employer.
body:
What exactly is the AI doing when a background check vendor says its screening is AI powered? In most products it is not deciding whether to hire anyone. It is reading messy court records, matching them to the right person, translating charge language and sorting results against rules the employer wrote. Knowing which of those jobs the software does, and which still belong to a person, is the difference between a faster check and a compliance problem.

What an AI background check is

An AI background check is a conventional employment screening report (criminal records, identity, employment and education verification, driving records) in which machine learning or language models handle parts of the collection, matching and review. Checkr, for example, describes its Checkr AI as decoding messy record data so that decisions can be defended. The legal framework does not change because software is involved: in the US the report is still a consumer report under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and the employer still needs a permissible purpose, a clear disclosure and the candidate's written authorization, as Checkr's compliance team explains in its guide to FCRA permissible purpose.

Where the AI sits in the process

StepWhat AI typically doesWho decides
IdentityCompares ID documents and selfies, flags mismatchesVendor rules, with human review of failures
Record searchReads court data, normalizes names, dates and charge textVendor, under its accuracy procedures
MatchingScores whether a record belongs to this candidateVendor, with manual checks on weak matches
ClassificationMaps charges to categories such as violent, theft or trafficVendor model; employer can review
AdjudicationApplies the employer's written criteria and routes resultsEmployer
Adverse actionSends notices on scheduleEmployer, after individual review

Identity is where AI has grown fastest, largely because of fraud. Certn says its identity verification checks candidates biometrically against more than 13,500 identity document types. That matters as remote hiring makes impersonation easier; our explainer on deepfake job candidates covers the interview side of the same problem.

Adjudication: the part to watch

Adjudication means deciding what a record means for a particular job. Vendors increasingly automate it. Checkr's adjudication product is pitched at teams dealing with dated records, confusing charge language and changing rules, and its Assess tool says customers can spend as little as one hour per week on adjudication by letting software sort results against their criteria.

Automation here is useful when it clears the large majority of reports that contain nothing relevant, and when it applies a written policy the same way every time. It becomes risky when the rules themselves are too broad, such as excluding every conviction regardless of age or relevance, because software then applies a bad policy at scale. Fair chance laws make this concrete: the National Employment Law Project counts 37 states and roughly 200 localities with fair chance hiring policies, many of which require an individualized look at the offense, the time since it happened and the job.

The steps software cannot skip

If a report could lead you to reject a candidate, the FCRA process still runs on a human timeline. Checkr's adverse action guide lists it: send a pre adverse action notice with a copy of the report, wait a reasonable period so the candidate can dispute errors or provide context, then send the final notice if you proceed. An AI system can draft and time these notices. It cannot replace the review that happens between them, and a candidate's explanation of a record is exactly the kind of context a model will not have.

Accuracy obligations also stay with the screening company. When a model matches a record to the wrong person with a similar name, the candidate's dispute right is the safeguard, so make sure your vendor's dispute process is fast and that your team pauses the decision while it runs.

Questions to ask a vendor

  • Which steps use machine learning, and which use fixed rules?
  • How does the system decide that a record belongs to this candidate, and what happens on a weak match?
  • Can we see and edit the adjudication criteria, and are changes logged?
  • What share of reports are reviewed by a person before results reach us?
  • Has the vendor tested outcomes for disparities by race, sex or age? Our guide to AI bias in hiring explains what such testing looks like.
  • How are candidate disputes handled, and how long do they take?

Some local rules on automated hiring tools may also apply, depending on how the product is used and where you hire. The NYC Local Law 144 explainer and our summary of the Colorado AI Act are good starting points for that conversation with counsel.

Bottom line

AI makes background checks faster mostly by cleaning up data and clearing routine reports. The judgment calls, the fairness of your criteria and the adverse action steps remain the employer's job, and the best vendors design their products around that line rather than blurring it.

faq.q: Are AI background checks legal?
faq.a: Yes. Using software to collect and sort records does not change the rules. The report is still a consumer report under the FCRA, so disclosure, written authorization and the adverse action process all apply.

faq.q: Can an AI reject a candidate based on a background check?
faq.a: Software can flag or route a report, but before rejecting someone the employer must send a pre adverse action notice with the report, give the candidate time to respond and then send a final notice. Many fair chance laws also require an individual assessment.

faq.q: How does AI help with identity fraud in hiring?
faq.a: Identity tools compare government ID documents with a live selfie and check document security features. Certn, for example, says it verifies against more than 13,500 identity document types.

faq.q: What is adjudication in a background check?
faq.a: Adjudication is the review of a report against the employer's written criteria to decide whether a record is relevant to the job. Vendors such as Checkr offer tools that automate the routine part of this review.

faq.q: Do AI background checks reduce bias?
faq.a: They can make decisions more consistent, but only if the criteria are fair. Automated rules that exclude broad categories of records apply that exclusion to every candidate, so test outcomes and review the policy regularly.

title: Recruiting chatbots: what they do, where they help and what to check before you buy
seoTitle: Recruiting Chatbots Explained
description: What recruiting chatbots do in 2026: FAQs, chat to apply, knockout screening and interview scheduling, the difference between scripted and generative bots, legal and fairness checks and a buyer checklist.
short: A recruiting chatbot is software that talks with job seekers by text to answer questions, take applications, ask screening questions and book interviews. It works best for high volume hourly hiring and needs clear rules, human hand off and outcome audits.
body:
Short version: a recruiting chatbot is software that holds a text conversation with job seekers so a recruiter does not have to. It answers questions, collects an application, asks knockout questions and books interviews, usually over SMS, a careers site widget or a messaging app. The good ones save hourly hiring teams a great deal of time. The bad ones trap candidates in a loop of scripted replies. The difference is mostly in how you configure and supervise them.

What a recruiting chatbot actually does

Most products combine four jobs. They answer frequently asked questions about pay, shifts, benefits and location. They let someone apply by chatting instead of filling in a long form. They screen with a few required questions, such as age for a role with a minimum, work authorization, availability or a license. And they schedule interviews by offering open slots from a hiring manager's calendar. Our explainers on AI interview scheduling and AI screening for hourly jobs go deeper on the last two.

Vendor pages show how this looks in practice. Paradox says candidates can apply and screen by text through SMS, WhatsApp or Facebook Messenger without creating an account, and pause and resume later. Sense pitches its AI chatbot as a 24/7 digital recruiter with smart FAQs about culture and benefits. Phenom's Talent Companion recommends specific roles in the chat and lets the person apply and book an interview in the same conversation.

Scripted bots versus generative assistants

Older chatbots follow decision trees: every question and answer is written in advance, and anything off script gets a fallback reply. They are predictable and easy to audit, but they break as soon as a candidate asks something unexpected.

Newer assistants use large language models to understand free text and write replies. That makes conversations feel natural and lets the bot answer questions it was never explicitly given, drawing on job descriptions and policy documents. The risk is that it can also answer wrongly with confidence. A generative bot that invents a pay rate or promises a schedule creates a real problem. The safest designs let the model handle language while hard rules control anything that decides eligibility or makes a commitment.

Where chatbots work well and where they do not

They shine in high volume hourly hiring: retail, restaurants, warehouses, call centers and healthcare support roles where hundreds of people apply, most of them on a phone, and speed decides who gets hired. Humanly, for example, markets itself to high volume hiring teams and pairs chat with screening, interviews and scheduling.

They add less for senior or specialist roles. A staff engineer or a finance director is rarely going to apply through a chat widget, and the questions that matter are about the team and the problem, which a recruiter should answer. For those searches, sourcing and personal outreach matter far more than conversation automation.

Fairness, disclosure and the law

A chatbot that screens people out is making an employment decision, so the same rules apply as for any other selection step. Knockout questions should be job related and consistent with business necessity. Watch for questions that act as proxies for protected traits, and test outcomes by group, as explained in our guide to AI bias in hiring. Depending on where you hire, laws such as New York City's bias audit rule or the EU AI Act may apply to automated screening. Tell candidates they are talking to software and give them an easy way to reach a person, including an accommodation route for anyone who cannot use the chat.

What to check before you buy

  • ATS integration. Does every answer, status change and booked interview write back to your applicant tracking system, or does someone copy it over by hand?
  • Channels. SMS is the default for hourly candidates. Check which messaging apps and languages are supported and how text consent is captured.
  • Control over answers. Can you lock pay, benefits and policy answers to approved text, and review every transcript?
  • Hand off to a human. How fast can a candidate reach a recruiter, and does the recruiter see the full conversation?
  • Reporting. Look for drop off by step, time to interview and outcomes by location and group.

Some teams find their real bottleneck is not conversation at all but the pile of applicants already sitting in the ATS. In that case tools that rank existing applicants against the role may help more than a chatbot, since recruiters decide whom to contact. For a broader look at how automation affects applicants, see AI and candidate experience.

The bottom line

A recruiting chatbot is worth it when you have volume, mobile applicants and simple, consistent screening rules. Configure it so the rules are explicit, keep humans one tap away, audit the outcomes and it will mostly be an improvement for candidates who would otherwise wait days for a reply.

faq.q: What is a recruiting chatbot?
faq.a: Software that holds a text conversation with candidates on a careers site, by SMS or in a messaging app, to answer questions, collect applications, screen with set questions and schedule interviews.

faq.q: Are recruiting chatbots legal?
faq.a: Yes, but screening questions they ask are a selection step. Keep them job related, disclose that candidates are talking to software, offer a human and an accommodation route, and check local rules on automated hiring tools.

faq.q: Do candidates like recruiting chatbots?
faq.a: Hourly applicants often prefer fast answers and text based scheduling. Frustration comes from bots that cannot answer off script questions or offer no way to reach a person.

faq.q: Will a chatbot replace recruiters?
faq.a: No. It removes repetitive messaging and scheduling, but recruiters still handle judgment calls, offers, hiring manager relationships and specialist searches.

title: AI video interviews: how recorded and AI led video screens work, what the law requires and what candidates think
seoTitle: AI Video Interviews Explained
description: What an AI video interview is in 2026: one way recorded screens, AI led conversations and AI assisted calls, what the software scores, the Illinois AI Video Interview Act, candidate survey data and questions to ask vendors.
short: An AI video interview is a video screen in which software transcribes, asks or scores the answers. The three common formats carry different legal and candidate experience risks, and Illinois requires notice, consent and deletion on request.
body:
Short version: an AI video interview is a recorded or live video screen in which software, not only a person, does part of the work. Sometimes the AI just transcribes and summarizes what the candidate said. Sometimes it asks the questions itself. In the most controversial setup, a candidate records answers alone to a webcam and a model scores the recording before any human watches it. Those three setups carry very different risks, so the first job for any employer is to know which one it is buying.

Three kinds of AI video interview

One way recorded interviews with AI scoring. The candidate gets a link, reads or hears a question, records an answer within a time limit and moves to the next prompt. The platform transcribes the answers and rates them against a rubric, then ranks the pool for a recruiter. This is the format most people mean when they search for the term, and the one candidates complain about most.

AI led conversational interviews. Instead of fixed prompts, an AI agent asks follow up questions based on what the candidate just said. Some of these run on camera, many run on voice only. The output is usually a transcript, a summary and a score per competency.

Human interviews with AI assistance. A recruiter or hiring manager runs a normal video call and an AI tool takes notes, tags answers to the scorecard and drafts feedback. The person still asks the questions and decides. Our explainer on AI note takers for interviews covers this category in depth.

What the software actually evaluates

Modern vendors mostly score the words. Speech is converted to text, and a language model compares each answer to the competencies and example answers the employer wrote for the role. A good rubric says what a strong, acceptable and weak answer to each question contains, which makes the score explainable.

Older products also analyzed facial movement, tone of voice and word choice as proxies for traits. That approach drew sustained criticism from researchers and regulators because the link between a candidate's expression on a webcam and job performance was never well established, and because it can penalize people with disabilities, accents or poor lighting. Ask any vendor in writing whether its model uses visual or vocal signals at all. If the answer is anything other than a clear no, you need to understand exactly what is measured and why.

How candidates feel about it in 2026

Candidate tolerance is lower than most buyers assume. The Greenhouse 2026 Candidate AI Interview Report, which surveyed 2,950 job seekers in the United States, United Kingdom, Ireland, Germany and Australia, found that 63% of US respondents had already faced an AI interview. Yet 38% of US candidates said they had withdrawn from a process because it included one, and another 12% said they would if required.

The single biggest reason for walking away, cited by 33% of US respondents, was a pre recorded video interview scored by AI with no human present. Lack of disclosure was close behind: 70% said AI evaluation was not clearly disclosed before their latest AI interview, and 21% only found out once it began. Silence afterward made it worse, since 51% of those who finished an AI interview never received an outcome. On the positive side, 46% wanted the option to ask for a human interview instead, a feature that costs little to offer. More data on this sits in our AI and candidate experience explainer.

The legal checklist

Illinois has the most specific rule. The Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act (820 ILCS 42) requires an employer that uses AI to analyze video interviews to tell each applicant beforehand, explain how the AI works and what general characteristics it evaluates, and get consent before the interview. Videos may only be shared with people whose expertise is needed to evaluate the applicant, and on request they must be deleted within 30 days, including copies held by vendors. Employers that rely solely on AI analysis to decide who gets an in person interview must also collect and report demographic data.

Other rules overlap. New York City's Local Law 144 requires a bias audit and notice for automated employment decision tools; see our Local Law 144 guide. Colorado and the EU AI Act treat hiring AI as high risk, which we cover in the Colorado AI Act and EU AI Act explainers. Disability law also applies everywhere: a candidate who cannot complete a timed webcam recording needs a reasonable alternative.

Where AI video interviews earn their place

  • High applicant volume with a clear rubric. Hundreds of applicants for customer service, retail or graduate roles, where the first screen tests a handful of predictable competencies.
  • Time zones and shift workers. Candidates can respond at midnight or on a break instead of trading voicemails with a recruiter.
  • Consistency. Every applicant gets the same questions in the same order, which is easier to audit than a dozen recruiters improvising phone screens.

They work poorly for senior, specialist or scarce talent. A sought after engineer or nurse who is asked to record answers to a webcam before speaking to a person often just stops responding.

Questions to ask a vendor

  1. Is scoring based only on transcript content, or also on face, voice or video signals?
  2. Can we see the rubric and the reason behind each score?
  3. Does a person review every AI recommendation before a candidate is rejected?
  4. Do you support Illinois notice, consent and 30 day deletion, and do you delete your own copies?
  5. Can candidates request a human interview or an accessible format?
  6. Has an independent auditor tested the tool for adverse impact, and can we read the summary?
  7. Can we turn off video and run the same screen by voice or text?

Video or voice?

For many first round screens the camera adds risk without adding signal. If what you need is a consistent structured conversation, a voice only screen avoids the appearance and lighting issues that make video scoring contentious. Noon's AI interviewer, for example, runs voice screens from an emailed link and returns a transcript and a next round recommendation to the team. Whichever format you pick, keep the decision with a person, disclose the AI in the invitation, and tell every candidate what happened next. Our overview of AI interviewers compares the wider category.

faq.q: What is an AI video interview?
faq.a: A video screening interview in which AI transcribes and summarizes answers, asks the questions itself, or scores recorded answers against a rubric before a recruiter reviews the results.

faq.q: Does AI judge facial expressions in video interviews?
faq.a: Most current vendors say they score the transcript only, but older tools analyzed facial and vocal signals. Ask the vendor in writing which signals the model uses.

faq.q: Is it legal to use AI to score video interviews?
faq.a: Yes in most places, with conditions. Illinois requires notice, an explanation of how the AI works, consent and deletion within 30 days on request. New York City requires a bias audit and notice for automated decision tools.

faq.q: Can a candidate refuse an AI video interview?
faq.a: In Illinois an employer may not use AI to evaluate an applicant who has not consented. Elsewhere, offering a human or accessible alternative is good practice and may be required for applicants with disabilities.

faq.q: How do I do well in an AI video interview?
faq.a: Answer the question asked with a specific example, keep to the time limit and speak clearly. Content matters most because most tools now score the transcript.

title: AI onboarding: what it automates from offer to day 90, where it helps and where people still matter
seoTitle: AI Onboarding Explained
description: What AI onboarding is in 2026: preboarding, provisioning workflows, new hire question assistants and agentic 30, 60 and 90 day plans, plus Gallup onboarding data, privacy questions and what AI should not do.
short: AI onboarding uses machine learning and generative AI to assign onboarding tasks, answer new hire questions and build ramp plans. It works best on coordination problems and needs human ownership of policy answers, eligibility checks and any evaluation of new hires.
body:
Picture a new hire's first Monday. The laptop is not ready, the manager is in meetings, the benefits form asks questions nobody explained, and the new hire spends the afternoon reading a handbook PDF. Gallup reports that only 12% of US employees say their company does a good job of onboarding. AI onboarding is the attempt to fix the parts of that Monday that are coordination problems, by letting software assemble tasks, answer routine questions and nudge the right people at the right time.

What AI onboarding means

AI onboarding is the use of machine learning and generative AI inside the onboarding process, from the signed offer to the end of the new hire's first few months. It usually sits on top of ordinary onboarding software, which already handles checklists, e signatures and task assignment. The AI layer adds three things: it decides which tasks apply to which person, it writes or answers in natural language, and in newer agentic products it takes actions such as creating accounts or scheduling meetings without a person clicking each step. Our explainer on agentic AI vs generative AI covers that difference in more detail.

Where it shows up in the first 90 days

Before day one. Preboarding is the stretch between a signed offer and the start date, when new hires are most likely to get cold feet. AI tools personalize welcome messages, collect forms, and build a schedule for the first week from the role, team and location.

Paperwork and provisioning. Workflow engines trigger equipment orders, system access and payroll setup. HiBob describes lifecycle triggered onboarding workflows with logic based on role and location, which is the rules based foundation most AI features build on.

Questions. A chat assistant trained on the handbook and benefits documents answers where to find the parking policy or how to enroll a dependent, so the HR inbox gets fewer repeats. This works like the recruiting chatbots candidates meet earlier in the funnel, with the same risk of confident wrong answers.

Ramp plans. Enboarder markets agentic AI that builds personalized 30, 60 and 90 day plans and supports frontline onboarding on mobile. Workday positions AI agents inside its onboarding product as part of its wider talent management suite.

Why employers care

Gallup's research ties good onboarding to retention and satisfaction: employees who had exceptional onboarding were 2.6 times as likely to be extremely satisfied with their workplace, and only 29% of new hires say they feel fully prepared and supported to excel in their role after onboarding. Most of what goes wrong is not complicated. A manager forgets a check in, or IT gets the request late. Automation is good at exactly that kind of failure.

For high volume and hourly employers there is a second reason. When hundreds of people start each month across many sites, HR cannot hand hold each one. Mobile first onboarding with automated reminders is often the difference between a new hire showing up for the second shift and not. The same logic applies earlier in the funnel, covered in AI screening for hourly jobs.

What AI should not do in onboarding

Replace the manager. The welcome, the first one on one and the explanation of what good work looks like still need a person. AI can schedule and prompt those conversations, not hold them.

Give unchecked policy or legal answers. A chatbot that invents a leave policy or misstates a benefit creates real liability. Limit it to approved documents, show the source for each answer and route anything about pay, leave or accommodations to a human.

Handle employment eligibility on its own. Identity and work authorization steps in the US have specific federal rules about who examines documents and when. Software can collect and track them, but HR should own the verification and check current government guidance.

Quietly evaluate new hires. Some tools score engagement or predict who is likely to leave. Once AI output feeds decisions about a person's job, rules on automated employment decisions may apply. See our explainers on the Colorado AI Act and the EU AI Act.

Data and privacy

Onboarding collects some of the most sensitive data an employer holds: tax forms, bank details, identity documents, emergency contacts and sometimes health information for benefits. Before turning on any AI feature, ask the vendor whether new hire data is used to train shared models, where it is stored, who can see chat transcripts and how long they are kept. Keep sensitive fields out of the generative AI layer unless the vendor can explain exactly how they are protected.

How to start

Map your current onboarding steps and mark which ones are coordination, which are information and which are relationship. Automate coordination first, since it carries the least risk. Add a question answering assistant only once your documents are current, because it will repeat whatever they say. Measure what changes: time to productivity, first 90 day turnover and the number of questions reaching HR. If those numbers do not move, the tool is decoration. Our overview of AI in HR puts onboarding next to the other HR processes where AI is used.

faq.q: What is AI onboarding?
faq.a: It is the use of AI inside employee onboarding to personalize tasks, answer new hire questions, trigger account and equipment setup and build ramp plans from offer acceptance through the first months.

faq.q: Can AI replace HR in onboarding?
faq.a: No. It can remove repetitive coordination and routine questions, but managers still need to welcome and coach new hires, and HR should own policy answers and employment eligibility steps.

faq.q: Is AI onboarding covered by AI hiring laws?
faq.a: Routine task automation usually is not the focus of those laws. Tools that score or predict outcomes for individual employees can fall under rules on automated employment decisions, so review them with counsel.

title: AI resume parsing: how software turns a CV into data, where it breaks and how to test it
seoTitle: AI Resume Parsing Explained
description: How AI resume parsing works in 2026: what a parser extracts, how rules gave way to machine learning and language models, the layouts and dates that still break it, fairness and privacy questions, and a buyer's test plan.
short: AI resume parsing converts a resume or CV into structured fields such as titles, employers, dates and skills so recruiting software can search and match it. Current parsers handle standard documents well but still miss data in designed layouts, unusual dates and less common languages, so test them on your own applicants.
body:
Resume parsing is the least glamorous AI in recruiting and one of the most consequential. Before a ranking model, a chatbot or a recruiter's search can do anything with an application, software has to turn a PDF or Word file into structured fields: name, contact details, employers, titles, dates, schools, skills. If that step drops a job or misreads a date, every later step inherits the mistake. The short verdict is that modern AI parsers are good at standard resumes in common languages and still worth testing on the messy ones your applicants actually send.

What a resume parser does

A parser reads an unstructured document and returns a structured record, usually as JSON or XML, that an applicant tracking system, CRM or job board can store and search. A typical output has a contact block, a list of positions with employer, title, start and end dates and description, an education list, and a skills list. Better parsers also normalize what they find: they map "Sr. SWE" and "Senior Software Engineer" to one title, link a skill to a taxonomy entry, and calculate total years of experience. Many also parse job descriptions with the same engine so a resume and an opening can be compared field by field. That comparison is the basis of most automated matching, which our explainer on AI in applicant tracking systems covers.

The industry has tried to standardize the output for decades. The HR Open Standards Consortium, founded in 1999, maintains nonprofit specifications for exchanging HR data, including candidate records, so that a parser and an ATS from different vendors can speak the same schema.

From rules to machine learning to language models

Early parsers relied on keyword lists and layout rules: find the word "Experience", treat what follows as jobs, look for patterns that resemble dates. They broke on two column layouts, tables, headers and anything written in an unexpected order. The next generation used statistical models trained on labeled resumes to recognize entities such as company names and titles in context, which handled variety much better. The current generation adds large language models that can read a resume more like a person does, infer that a line under a company name is a title even without a label, and summarize a career in plain language.

Vendors in this market describe that shift in their own positioning. Textkernel now sells the Sovren parser it combined with its own technology, pitching fast, multilingual resume and job parsing. HireAbility markets ALEX, a multilingual parser that turns resumes, CVs and vacancies into structured data for ATS, CRM and HR systems. RChilli has moved from parsing toward AI agents that run from resume intake to matching inside Oracle Recruiting Cloud and SAP SuccessFactors. Daxtra, long known for parsing in staffing software, now sells a broader automation platform for agencies. The parser is increasingly a component inside something larger rather than a product on its own.

Where parsing still goes wrong

Layout. Multi column designs, text inside images, icons for phone and email, and skills shown as bar charts are still the most common causes of lost data. A designer's portfolio resume can come out with half its content missing.

Dates and gaps. "2019 to present", "Summer 2021" and overlapping contract roles confuse calculations of tenure. A parser that guesses wrong can make a candidate look like a job hopper or hide a gap that a recruiter would want to ask about.

Titles and employers. Internal titles, staffing agency placements listed under the client's name, and acquisitions where the employer changed names all produce records that look clean but are wrong.

Languages and formats. Accuracy usually drops outside the vendor's core languages and for local conventions such as photos, date of birth or national ID numbers, which some countries expect on a CV and others forbid employers from using.

Generated text. Language model parsers can fill a missing field with something plausible. Ask whether the output is extracted from the document or inferred, and whether inferred values are flagged.

Why parsing matters for fairness and compliance

Parsing looks neutral, but it shapes what a screening model sees. If a parser misreads foreign degrees or drops employment at organizations it does not recognize, the candidates affected tend to share a background, and the error becomes a pattern. That is one route by which bias in AI hiring enters a process before any scoring happens. Where a tool scores or ranks candidates using parsed data, rules such as New York City Local Law 144 may require a bias audit of the whole tool, so keep the parser in scope when you document how candidates are evaluated.

Data protection is the other issue. A parser processes everything in the document, including details you never asked for. Check where the vendor processes and stores files, how long it keeps them, and whether it uses customer resumes to train its models.

What candidates should know

From the applicant's side, the advice is simple and backed by vendors that test resumes against ATS software, such as Jobscan: use a single column layout, standard section headings, real text rather than images, and dates in a consistent format. Our explainer on ATS resumes and AI screening covers what happens after parsing, when software compares the record to the job.

How to test a parser before you buy

Do not rely on a demo with clean sample resumes. Pull 50 to 100 real applications from your own ATS, with permission and personal data handled properly, and include the hard cases: designed resumes, scanned PDFs, non English CVs, career changers, contractors with many short roles. Run them through each parser and compare against a hand checked version of the same fields. Measure field level accuracy for the fields you use most, usually titles, employers, dates and skills, and time how long a recruiter spends fixing records afterward. That correction time is the cost a vendor's accuracy claim is meant to cover.

Finally, ask what happens when parsing fails. The best systems keep the original document attached and visible, flag low confidence fields, and let a recruiter correct the record so the fix improves search. A parser that fails silently is worse than one that admits it is unsure.

faq.q: What is resume parsing?
faq.a: It is the automatic extraction of information from a resume into structured fields, such as contact details, work history, education and skills, so that an ATS or CRM can store, search and match it.

faq.q: Is AI resume parsing accurate?
faq.a: On standard single column resumes in widely used languages it is usually accurate for core fields. Accuracy drops on designed layouts, scanned files, overlapping dates and less common languages, which is why testing on your own applications matters.

faq.q: Does a resume parser decide who gets hired?
faq.a: Not by itself. It produces the data that screening and matching tools use, so its errors can affect rankings later in the process even though it does not score anyone.

faq.q: How can candidates make a resume easier to parse?
faq.a: Use one column, standard headings such as Experience and Education, real text instead of images or charts, and a consistent date format.

title: AI generated resumes: how common they are, why detectors fail and what recruiters should check instead
seoTitle: AI Generated Resumes Explained for Recruiters
description: What AI generated resumes are, how many candidates use AI to write them according to 2024 and 2025 Gartner surveys, why AI text detectors are unreliable, where fabrication risk sits and how to adjust screening and policy.
short: An AI generated resume is one drafted or edited with a language model. Gartner found 39 percent of candidates used AI while applying and 54 percent of those used it for resume text. Polishing is not fraud; detectors are unreliable, so verify specifics, identity and skills instead.
body:
If half of your applicants used a chatbot to write their resume, would you be able to tell, and should you care? Gartner's answer to the first part is that the share is already large. A Gartner survey of 3,290 job candidates in late 2024 found that 39 percent used AI during the application process, and 54 percent of those used it to generate resume text. The second part is the interesting one. An AI generated resume is not automatically dishonest, and treating it as fraud creates more problems than it solves. This explainer covers what the term means, why detection is unreliable, where the real risks sit and how to adjust screening.

What counts as an AI generated resume

The phrase covers a wide range. At one end, a candidate pastes a draft into a chatbot and asks it to fix grammar and tighten bullet points. In the middle, a candidate asks the model to rewrite the whole document for a specific job description, which pulls the posting's keywords into the text. At the far end, a resume is invented: employers, titles or skills the person never had, sometimes attached to a fabricated identity. Only that last group is a fraud problem. The first two are closer to what candidates once paid a resume writer to do.

The same Gartner research shows AI use extends beyond the resume. Among candidates who used AI, 50 percent generated cover letter text, 36 percent writing samples and 29 percent answers to assessment questions. Those last two matter more to hiring quality than a polished summary paragraph, because they are meant to show what the candidate can do alone.

Why detectors are a weak test

Many recruiters reach for an AI text detector. The track record is poor. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier on July 20, 2023, citing its low rate of accuracy. Resumes make the job harder: they are short, formulaic and full of stock phrases that humans wrote long before language models existed. A detector that flags "results driven professional" will flag most of your pipeline, including people who wrote every word themselves, and it can also flag candidates whose writing is simply formal. That is a fairness risk as well as a waste of time, which our explainer on AI bias in hiring discusses in more detail.

What actually changes for screening

The practical effect of AI writing is that resumes now look more alike and match job descriptions more closely. Keyword overlap, once a rough proxy for fit, says less than it did. If your screening relies on keyword scoring in an applicant tracking system, expect more applicants to pass the first filter, and see our page on ATS resumes and AI screening for how those filters work. Parsing is usually unaffected: clean, model written text in a standard layout is easy for software to read, as the AI resume parsing explainer explains.

What becomes more valuable is evidence that cannot be generated in seconds:

  • Verifiable specifics. Named systems, dates, team sizes and outcomes that a reference or a work sample can confirm.
  • Live conversation. A short phone or video screen where the candidate expands on two resume claims.
  • Supervised or structured work samples. Tasks designed so that a pasted answer is obvious, or done in the interview.

Where the fraud risk really is

Fabrication is rarer than AI polishing in the Gartner figures, but each case costs far more. In a second quarter 2025 survey of 3,000 candidates, Gartner found that 6 percent admitted to interview fraud, either posing as someone else or having someone pose as them, and the firm predicts that by 2028 one in four candidate profiles worldwide will be fake. Gartner's Jamie Kohn said candidate fraud creates cybersecurity risks that can be far more serious than a bad hire. Those cases need identity checks and consistency checks across the process, which our explainer on deepfake job candidates covers. They do not need a detector run on every resume.

Writing a policy candidates can follow

Gartner recommends that employers explain what acceptable AI use looks like and how fraud is detected. A workable policy usually says three things: using AI to draft or edit application materials is fine; every claim must be true and the candidate must be able to discuss it; and assessments or work samples must be the candidate's own unless the instructions say otherwise. Publishing this on the careers page sets expectations and gives recruiters a fair basis for rejecting fabricated applications.

A short checklist for recruiting teams

SignalWhat it usually meansWhat to do
Generic, polished languageAI editing, or a templateIgnore; judge the specifics
Resume mirrors the job post word for wordTailoring with a chatbotProbe two claims in the screen
Dates, employers or titles that do not reconcilePossible fabricationVerify employment before interviews
Different person or voice between stagesPossible identity fraudRun identity verification

The bottom line: assume many resumes have had AI help, stop treating writing quality as a signal of competence, and put verification effort where it pays off, on identity, employment history and the skills the job actually requires.

faq.q: Is it wrong for candidates to use AI to write a resume?
faq.a: Not in itself. Using AI to draft or edit is similar to using a resume writer. The problem is false information, such as invented employers, titles or skills.

faq.q: Can recruiters detect AI generated resumes?
faq.a: Not reliably. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in 2023 because of low accuracy, and resumes are short and formulaic, which makes false positives common.

faq.q: How many job seekers use AI on their resume?
faq.a: In a Gartner survey of 3,290 candidates in late 2024, 39 percent used AI in the application process, and 54 percent of those used it to generate resume or CV text.

faq.q: What should replace resume keyword screening?
faq.a: Short live screens that probe specific claims, structured work samples and verification of employment history and identity for finalists.

faq.q: Should employers publish an AI policy for applicants?
faq.a: Yes. Gartner advises employers to explain acceptable AI use and how fraud is detected, which sets expectations and supports fair decisions.

faq.q: Are fake candidates common?
faq.a: Gartner found 6 percent of candidates admitted to interview fraud in 2025 and predicts that by 2028 one in four candidate profiles worldwide will be fake.

title: Illinois AI Video Interview Act: notice, consent, deletion and reporting rules explained
seoTitle: Illinois AI Video Interview Act Explained for Employers
description: What the Illinois Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act (820 ILCS 42) requires: who it covers, the notice, explanation and consent steps, the 30 day deletion rule, demographic reporting, and how the 2026 Human Rights Act AI amendment adds to it.
short: The Illinois AI Video Interview Act covers employers that use AI to analyze recorded interviews for Illinois jobs. They must notify applicants, explain how the AI works, get consent, share videos only with evaluators, delete them within 30 days on request, and report race data if AI alone decides who advances.
body:
Illinois was the first state to write a law specifically about artificial intelligence in job interviews. The Artificial Intelligence Video Interview Act, codified at 820 ILCS 42, took effect on January 1, 2020, and it is still short enough to read in five minutes. It does not ban AI scoring of recorded interviews. It sets four duties for employers that use it: tell candidates, explain the system, get consent, and limit what happens to the videos afterward. A 2022 amendment added demographic reporting for employers that let the AI make the cut on its own.

Who the law covers

The Act applies to an employer that asks applicants to record video interviews and uses an artificial intelligence analysis of those videos when considering applicants for positions based in Illinois. Three conditions have to line up: the interview is recorded rather than live, software analyzes it, and the job is located in Illinois. Where the employer is headquartered does not matter. A Texas company hiring for a Chicago warehouse role is covered; an Illinois company hiring for a Denver role is not, at least under this statute.

A live video call with a human interviewer and no AI analysis is outside the Act. So is a recorded interview that a recruiter simply watches. The trigger is software evaluating the recording.

The three steps before the interview

Section 5 requires the employer to do all of the following before asking the applicant to submit a video:

  1. Notify the applicant that artificial intelligence may be used to analyze the interview and consider their fitness for the position.
  2. Explain how the artificial intelligence works and what general types of characteristics it uses to evaluate applicants.
  3. Obtain consent from the applicant to be evaluated by the program as described.

The Act then adds a hard rule: an employer may not use artificial intelligence to evaluate applicants who have not consented. In practice, that means the recording workflow needs a path for people who decline, such as a live interview with a person, and the employer needs a record showing who agreed and to which explanation.

The statute does not define how detailed the explanation must be. Most employers rely on a plain language notice from the vendor describing what the model looks at, for example the content of answers rather than facial expressions. If your vendor cannot tell you what characteristics its system uses, you cannot meet the explanation duty.

What happens to the videos

Section 10 limits sharing. Applicant videos may go only to people whose expertise or technology is needed to evaluate the applicant's fitness for the role. Your AI vendor qualifies; a marketing team building a recruiting highlight reel does not.

Section 15 covers deletion. If an applicant asks, the employer must delete the interview within 30 days of receiving the request and instruct anyone else who received copies, including the vendor, to delete them too, along with all electronically generated backups. Those recipients must comply. Build that into the vendor contract, because the employer carries the duty even when the files sit on someone else's servers.

The 2022 demographic reporting rule

Section 20, added by Public Act 102-47 and effective January 1, 2022, applies only to employers that rely solely on an AI analysis of a video interview to decide who gets an in person interview. Those employers must collect the race and ethnicity of applicants who are and are not advanced after the AI review, and of applicants who are hired. They report the data to the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity every year by December 31, covering the 12 months ending November 30. The Department then analyzes it and reports to the Governor and General Assembly by July 1 on whether it shows racial bias.

The word solely matters. If a recruiter reviews every candidate the AI rejects, or the score is one input among several, the reporting duty arguably does not apply. Many employers keep a human review step partly for that reason.

How the 2026 Human Rights Act amendment fits in

Since January 1, 2026, Illinois has a second, broader AI rule for employers. Public Act 103-0804 amended the Illinois Human Rights Act to make it a civil rights violation to use artificial intelligence in recruitment, hiring, promotion and other employment decisions in a way that has the effect of discriminating against protected classes, or to use zip codes as a proxy for protected classes. It also requires employers to give employees notice when they use AI for those purposes, with details left to rules from the Illinois Department of Human Rights.

The two laws overlap but do different jobs. The Video Interview Act is narrow and procedural: notice, explanation, consent, sharing, deletion and reporting for recorded interviews. The Human Rights Act amendment is broad and outcome based: any AI used in employment decisions, judged by whether it produces discriminatory effects. An employer using AI video scoring for Illinois roles should plan for both.

A compliance checklist for Illinois roles

  • List every place your hiring process records video and every vendor that scores it.
  • Get a written description from each vendor of what its model evaluates, in language a candidate can understand.
  • Show notice and the explanation before the recording link, and capture consent with a timestamp.
  • Offer a non AI interview path to anyone who declines.
  • Put sharing limits and the 30 day deletion duty, including backups, into vendor contracts.
  • Decide whether any stage relies solely on AI; if so, set up race and ethnicity reporting by December 31.
  • Run a periodic adverse impact review so the Human Rights Act amendment does not catch you off guard.

For how these rules compare with other jurisdictions, see our explainers on New York City Local Law 144 bias audits and the Colorado AI Act, and our overview of AI video interviews for how the technology works.

This explainer summarizes the statute text published by the Illinois General Assembly and is not legal advice.

faq.q: Does the Illinois AI Video Interview Act apply to live Zoom interviews?
faq.a: Not on its own terms. It covers recorded video interviews that the employer analyzes with artificial intelligence. A live call with a human interviewer and no AI analysis falls outside it.

faq.q: Does the law apply to companies outside Illinois?
faq.a: Yes, if the position is based in Illinois. Coverage depends on where the job is, not where the employer is headquartered.

faq.q: How quickly must an employer delete an applicant's video?
faq.a: Within 30 days after the applicant asks, and the employer must tell anyone who received copies, including vendors, to delete them and their backups.

faq.q: Who has to report demographic data?
faq.a: Only employers that rely solely on AI analysis of video interviews to decide who gets an in person interview. They report race and ethnicity data to the Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity by December 31 each year.

faq.q: Is there a penalty section in the Act?
faq.a: The statute text does not include a specific penalty or private right of action provision. Employers should still treat it as binding and watch for overlapping claims under the Illinois Human Rights Act.

faq.q: What changed in Illinois in 2026?
faq.a: Public Act 103-0804, effective January 1, 2026, amended the Illinois Human Rights Act to prohibit AI use in employment decisions that has a discriminatory effect, bar zip codes as a proxy for protected classes, and require notice to employees when AI is used.

title: Mobley v. Workday: what the AI hiring bias lawsuit claims and where it stands in 2026
seoTitle: Mobley v. Workday Explained: The AI Hiring Bias Lawsuit and Where It Stands
description: Plain English guide to Mobley v. Workday: the age, race and disability claims against Workday's AI screening, the 2025 collective certification, the March 2026 opt in deadline and Workday's November 2026 decertification motion.
short: Mobley v. Workday is a federal lawsuit in Northern California claiming Workday's AI screening features discriminate against applicants by age, race and disability. A nationwide age collective was preliminarily certified in May 2025, the opt in window closed March 7, 2026, and in November 2026 Workday asked the court to decertify it. There is no ruling on the merits and no settlement.
body:
Mobley v. Workday is the first major federal lawsuit to test whether the company that sells an AI screening tool, not just the employer that uses it, can be liable for discrimination in hiring. It has not been decided. As of November 21, 2026 there is no ruling on whether Workday's tools actually discriminated, no settlement, and a pending fight over whether the case can stay a single nationwide action. What it has already done is survive the early motions that end most cases, which is why HR and talent acquisition teams that use any automated screening should understand it.

The case in one paragraph
