Derek Mobley, a job seeker over 40, filed the suit on February 21, 2023 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, case number 3:23-cv-00770, before Judge Rita F. Lin. According to a Holland & Knight client alert, he applied for more than 100 jobs at companies that use Workday's platform and was rejected every time. His complaint alleges that Workday's AI features, which score, sort, rank or screen applicants, discriminate on the basis of age, race and disability under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Workday has said the claims lack merit.

Why the vendor is the defendant

Discrimination law has traditionally targeted employers and employment agencies. Mobley's lawyers argue that Workday acts as an agent of the employers that use it, because its software makes or shapes decisions about who moves forward. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission filed an amicus brief in the case on April 9, 2024, under the same three statutes. The court initially dismissed the first complaint but allowed an amended one, and then denied Workday's motion to dismiss that version, letting the age claim proceed on a disparate impact theory. Disparate impact means the plaintiff does not have to prove anyone intended to discriminate, only that a practice falls harder on a protected group without enough business justification.

Timeline of key rulings

  • February 2023: complaint filed in the Northern District of California.
  • April 2024: EEOC files a brief supporting the theory that an AI vendor can be covered.
  • May 16, 2025: Judge Lin grants preliminary certification of a nationwide collective under the ADEA, covering applicants aged 40 and older who were denied employment recommendations through Workday's platform since September 24, 2020, per Holland & Knight.
  • Early 2026: the court authorizes notice to potential members. A March 2026 update from RM Compare reported an opt in deadline of March 7, 2026.
  • November 10, 2026: Workday asks the court to decertify the collective, arguing that each employer configures its screening differently, according to a Lawfold case tracker, which cites MLex reporting that more than 15,000 applicants opted in.

What a collective action is, and why the opt in matters

Age claims under the ADEA proceed as collective actions rather than ordinary class actions. Members are not included automatically; they must file a written consent to join. That is why the March 2026 deadline mattered: people who did not opt in are not part of this collective. If the court grants Workday's decertification motion, the opt in plaintiffs would not lose their claims outright, but each would generally have to pursue them separately, which changes the economics of the case for both sides. The plaintiffs also have a separate pending request to certify a class for other claims.

What employers using AI screening should do now

None of this creates a new rule yet, and this explainer is not legal advice. But the case has already shifted what careful buyers ask vendors.

  1. Map where automation decides. List every step where software scores, ranks, filters or auto rejects applicants, including knockout questions and recommendation features you may have switched on by default.
  2. Ask for adverse impact testing. Request the vendor's most recent analysis by age, race and sex, and ask how often it is repeated. Our guide to NYC Local Law 144 bias audits explains the format some vendors already publish.
  3. Keep a human in the loop for rejections. Automatic rejection based on a model score is the pattern at the center of Mobley. Review a sample of auto rejected applicants every month.
  4. Read the contract. Check indemnity, data access and audit rights so you can get the records you would need if a claim arrived.
  5. Track state law too. Colorado, Illinois and New York City already regulate parts of AI hiring; see our explainers on the Colorado AI Act and AI bias in hiring. For a wider checklist across tools, there is also a practical rundown of AI hiring compliance worth reading alongside your counsel's advice.

What to watch next

Three decisions will shape the outcome: whether Judge Lin keeps the collective together, whether a class is certified on the plaintiffs' separate motion, and what the evidence shows about how Workday's recommendation features actually performed for older applicants. Any of those rulings could prompt settlement talks, and any final judgment would likely be appealed. Whatever happens, the case has made vendor liability a standard question in AI hiring procurement.

faq.q: Is Mobley v. Workday settled?
faq.a: No. As of November 21, 2026 no settlement had been announced and the court had not ruled on whether Workday's tools discriminated. Workday's motion to decertify the age collective was pending.

faq.q: Can I still join the Workday lawsuit?
faq.a: Not this collective. The opt in deadline for the age discrimination collective was March 7, 2026. Anyone with a possible claim should speak to an employment lawyer about other options.

faq.q: Does the case mean employers cannot use AI to screen applicants?
faq.a: No. It tests whether vendors can share liability and whether specific features had a disparate impact. Employers can still use AI screening, but should test for adverse impact, keep human review of rejections and document how the tools are configured.

title: TRAIGA explained: what the Texas AI law means for hiring and recruiting in 2026
seoTitle: TRAIGA Explained: The Texas AI Law and Hiring
description: Plain English guide to TRAIGA, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act: what it bans, why it is narrower than Colorado's law for employers, how the attorney general enforces it and what recruiting teams should still do.
short: TRAIGA, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, took effect January 1, 2026. For private employers it bans developing or deploying AI with the intent to unlawfully discriminate, and says disparate impact alone does not prove that intent. It has no bias audit or candidate notice duty for private companies, no private right of action, and only the attorney general can enforce it.
body:
Texas passed one of the most talked about state AI laws of 2025, and recruiters in the state keep asking whether it changes how they can screen applicants. The short answer is: less than the headlines suggested. The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, usually shortened to TRAIGA, became effective on January 1, 2026. Its rules for private companies are mostly prohibitions on intentional misuse, not the audit and disclosure duties found in other laws. This explainer walks through what it covers, how it is enforced and where hiring teams still carry risk. It is not legal advice; the Texas Attorney General's own TRAIGA overview says the same about its summary.

What TRAIGA prohibits

According to the attorney general's overview, the act bars any person from developing or deploying an AI system that intentionally aims to incite self harm, harm to others or criminal activity, that is built with the sole intent to infringe constitutional rights, or that produces certain sexually explicit material involving minors or deepfakes. Several further rules apply only to governmental entities, such as bans on social scoring and on identifying people from biometric data gathered without consent.

The rule that matters most for recruiting reads, in the overview's words, that a person may not develop or deploy an AI system with the intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class in violation of state or federal law. The next sentence is the one employment lawyers quote: a disparate impact alone is not sufficient to demonstrate an intent to discriminate.

Why the intent standard matters for screening tools

Most worries about AI in hiring are about disparate impact: a resume ranker or video scoring model that, without anyone meaning it to, scores one group lower than another. Federal law and many state laws already treat a significant, unjustified adverse impact as potential discrimination. TRAIGA does not add a new claim on that basis. To violate the Texas act, a company would have to have built or used the system with the intent to discriminate.

That does not make adverse impact safe. Title VII, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act still apply in Texas, and the federal Mobley v. Workday case shows that disparate impact claims against AI screening can survive early motions. TRAIGA simply declines to layer a second, state level version of that claim on top.

What TRAIGA does not require from private employers

Compared with laws recruiters may already know, the Texas act is light on paperwork for private companies:

  • No bias audit. Unlike New York City Local Law 144, there is no annual independent audit of automated employment decision tools.
  • No candidate notice duty. The disclosure rule in the overview applies to governmental agencies whose AI systems interact with consumers, and to health care providers. The act's definition of consumer also excludes anyone acting in an employment context.
  • No impact assessment. The Colorado AI Act asks deployers of high risk systems to run impact assessments and give notices; TRAIGA has no equivalent for private employers.
  • No private lawsuits. The overview states plainly that TRAIGA does not provide a private right of action, so a rejected applicant cannot sue under it.

How the attorney general enforces it

The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce TRAIGA, unless it recommends that another state agency also act, and it may issue civil investigative demands. It can seek civil penalties, injunctions, attorney's fees and investigative costs. The overview lists penalty ranges of $10,000 to $12,000 for each violation a court finds curable, $80,000 to $200,000 for each violation found uncurable, and $2,000 to $40,000 for each day a violation continues. The overview also links to an online form where members of the public can file an AI complaint, which is how most investigations are likely to start.

What Texas hiring teams should still do

Because liability under TRAIGA turns on intent, the best protection is a record that shows you did not intend to discriminate and took reasonable steps to catch problems. In practice:

  1. Inventory your AI. List every tool that ranks, scores, screens or writes to candidates, including features switched on inside your applicant tracking system.
  2. Write down the purpose. For each tool, record what decision it supports and which job related criteria it uses. That document is your first answer to a civil investigative demand.
  3. Test for adverse impact anyway. Federal law still applies. Run selection rate comparisons at each stage, and see our explainer on AI bias in hiring for how.
  4. Keep a person on rejections. Human review of automated rejections is cheap insurance under every law in this area.
  5. Plan for other states. If you also recruit in Colorado, Illinois or New York City, the strictest rule usually becomes your baseline.

Who it applies to

The act reaches anyone who promotes, advertises or conducts business in Texas, produces a product or service used by Texas residents, or develops or deploys an AI system in the state. A staffing firm in another state that screens Texas applicants with AI, and a vendor selling screening software to Texas employers, are both likely in scope, so contracts with vendors should say who is responsible for testing and documentation.

faq.q: What is TRAIGA?
faq.a: TRAIGA is the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, a state law effective January 1, 2026 that prohibits certain intentional harmful uses of AI, adds duties for government agencies, and is enforced by the Texas Attorney General.

faq.q: Does TRAIGA ban AI resume screening in Texas?
faq.a: No. It bans developing or deploying AI with the intent to unlawfully discriminate. Screening tools remain legal, though federal anti discrimination law still applies to their results.

faq.q: Do Texas employers have to tell candidates they use AI?
faq.a: TRAIGA's disclosure rule applies to governmental agencies interacting with consumers and to health care providers, and its definition of consumer excludes people acting in an employment context. Other laws, such as Illinois rules on video interviews, may still require notice.

faq.q: Can a job applicant sue under TRAIGA?
faq.a: No. The attorney general's overview states that the act does not provide a private right of action. Enforcement belongs to the attorney general.

faq.q: What are the penalties under TRAIGA?
faq.a: The attorney general's overview lists $10,000 to $12,000 per curable violation, $80,000 to $200,000 per uncurable violation, and $2,000 to $40,000 per day for continuing violations.

title: AI interview assistants explained: the real time answer tools candidates use and how employers respond
seoTitle: AI Interview Assistant: What It Is and How Employers Respond
description: What an AI interview assistant is, how real time tools like Final Round AI, LockedIn AI and Interview Coder feed candidates answers during live interviews, what the 2025 Gartner data shows and what hiring teams can do.
short: An AI interview assistant is software that listens to a live job interview and suggests answers or code to the candidate in real time, often in a window hidden from screen sharing. Vendors such as Final Round AI, LockedIn AI and Interview Coder sell them to job seekers. Employers respond with clear AI use policies, deeper follow up questions, identity checks and in person rounds.
body:
A candidate shares their screen for a technical interview. The interviewer sees a code editor and a calm face. The candidate sees something else: a small window, invisible to the screen share, that listens to each question and drafts an answer within seconds. That window is an AI interview assistant, and in 2026 several companies sell one openly to job seekers. This explainer covers what these tools do, how they differ from interview practice apps, what they mean for hiring teams and which responses actually hold up.

What an AI interview assistant is

The term covers software that runs during a live interview and feeds the candidate suggested answers in real time. The vendors describe it plainly. Final Round AI calls its Interview CoPilot an AI interview assistant that hears the interview and privately suggests an answer in seconds, and says it is trusted by more than 10 million job seekers. LockedIn AI says its assistant listens to the interview, analyzes questions and provides real time answers, code solutions and coaching, claims more than one million users and advertises that its desktop app stays private when you share your screen. Interview Coder goes furthest, marketing itself as the number one undetectable AI for interviews, used by more than 150,000 candidates, with features that hide it from the dock, the activity monitor and screen recordings.

That last group of features is what separates an interview assistant from an AI interview practice tool. Practice tools run mock interviews before the real one. Assistants are built for the real one, and many are designed so the interviewer cannot tell.

How the tools work

  • Audio capture. The app transcribes the interviewer's voice from the call as it happens.
  • Context loading. Candidates upload a resume and job description in advance so suggested answers mention their own experience.
  • Answer generation. A language model drafts a spoken answer, a coding solution or an answer to a multiple choice assessment question.
  • Concealment. Overlay windows are excluded from screen sharing, and some apps offer a second device mode or let a remote helper watch the interview.

How common candidate AI use has become

Hard numbers on live interview assistance are scarce, but the surrounding data points one way. A Gartner press release from July 2025 reported that 39 percent of 3,290 candidates surveyed in late 2024 used AI during the application process, including 29 percent who used it to generate answers to assessment questions. In a separate survey of 3,000 candidates in the second quarter of 2025, 6 percent admitted to interview fraud, either posing as someone else or having someone else pose as them. Gartner's Jamie Kohn warned that candidate fraud creates cybersecurity risks far more serious than a bad hire. The same research found only 26 percent of candidates trust AI to evaluate them fairly, so suspicion runs in both directions.

Where employers are drawing the line

Some employers now publish their rules instead of guessing. Anthropic's guidance for candidates, last updated July 10, 2025, invites applicants to use its Claude assistant to polish a resume they drafted themselves and to research and practice before interviews. Take home assessments should be done without AI unless the instructions allow it, and live interviews are, in the company's words, all the candidate, with no AI assistance unless indicated. That three part split, encouraged for preparation, restricted for assessments, off limits live, is a useful template for any hiring team.

What hiring teams can do

  1. Publish an AI use policy on the careers page and in the interview invitation, so candidates know the rules before they start.
  2. Ask follow ups that go deeper, not wider. A generated answer to the first question is easy; explaining why a past decision was wrong, or changing a solution when constraints shift, is much harder to outsource in real time.
  3. Use work you can discuss. Have candidates walk through code or a document they produced earlier and defend the tradeoffs.
  4. Verify identity at the first live call and again at the final round, since Gartner's fraud figure is about impersonation as much as assistance. Our explainer on deepfake job candidates covers the identity side.
  5. Bring one round on site for roles where the cost of a bad hire is high, or use proctoring with the candidate's consent.

Detection software exists, but the vendors on the other side are tuning against it daily, and accusing a candidate on the strength of a suspicion invites complaints. Changing the interview design is more durable than trying to win an arms race. Teams that use AI themselves, such as AI interviewers for first round screens, should hold that process to the same transparency they ask of candidates; our guide chapter on candidate rights lists the disclosure rules that apply in some states.

The bottom line

AI interview assistants are popular, cheap and openly marketed as invisible. Hiring teams cannot ban them out of existence, but they can make them much less useful by stating clear rules, asking questions that reward real understanding and confirming who is on the call.

faq.q: What is an AI interview assistant?
faq.a: It is an app that runs during a live interview, transcribes the interviewer's questions and shows the candidate suggested answers or code solutions in real time.

faq.q: Is using an AI interview assistant cheating?
faq.a: It depends on the employer's rules. Many companies welcome AI for preparation but prohibit it during live interviews; Anthropic, for example, says live interviews should involve no AI assistance unless it says otherwise.

faq.q: Can interviewers detect AI interview assistants?
faq.a: Sometimes, through delayed answers, reading eye movements or answers that collapse under follow up questions. Several tools are designed to stay hidden from screen sharing, so interview design is more reliable than detection alone.

faq.q: How is an interview assistant different from interview practice software?
faq.a: Practice software runs mock interviews before the real one. An interview assistant is used during the real interview to supply answers.

faq.q: What should a company's AI interview policy say?
faq.a: State which stages allow AI, such as resume polishing and research, which stages do not, such as live interviews and timed assessments, and what happens if the rules are broken. Put it in the invitation, not just the careers page.

faq.q: Do AI interview assistants raise legal issues for employers?
faq.a: The tools are used by candidates, so the main legal exposure for employers comes from how they investigate suspected use. Apply the same process to every candidate and avoid rejecting someone on suspicion alone.

title: AI job interviews explained: the formats, what gets scored and the rules candidates should know
seoTitle: AI Job Interview: How It Works, What It Scores and Your Rights
description: What an AI job interview is in 2026: recorded video, conversational and chat formats, how answers are scored, the NYC, Illinois and Colorado rules, and how candidates and employers should prepare.
short: A plain guide to AI run first round interviews: formats, scoring, candidate rights and good practice for employers.
body:
Your interview invitation arrives at 9 p.m. with a link and a deadline of three days. There is no name of an interviewer, just a button that says Start. If that sounds familiar, you have been invited to an AI job interview: a first round run by software that asks the questions, records or transcribes your answers and passes a summary, and sometimes a score, to a human recruiter. This explainer is written for both sides of that link. It covers the three formats you are likely to meet, what the software is actually judging, the legal rules that apply in 2026 and how employers can run one without losing good candidates.

Three kinds of AI job interview

Recorded one way video. You see a question on screen, get a short time to think and record an answer. Nobody is live on the other end. This is the oldest format, and our AI video interviews explainer covers it in depth.

Conversational AI interviewer. A voice or avatar agent asks questions, listens and asks follow ups based on what you said. It behaves more like a phone screen than a quiz, and it can run by phone as well as by browser. See AI phone screening for the voice version used in hourly hiring.

Chat based screening. A text interview on the career site or by SMS asks about availability, certifications and work history, often before any human has looked at the application.

What the software is really evaluating

In most deployments the system is not reading your face. Several large vendors have dropped visual analysis, and the scoring that remains is built on the words you say. The software transcribes the answer, maps it to the competencies the employer configured for the role (for example customer handling, safety awareness or problem solving) and produces evidence notes against each one. Some products give a numeric rating; others only rank or summarize, leaving the judgment to the recruiter.

That has a practical meaning for candidates: structure beats polish. A clear example with a situation, the action you took and the result is easier for a transcript based model to match to a competency than a confident but general answer. Background, lighting and accent should not count, and if an employer cannot tell you that, ask.

Why employers use them

The main reason is timing. HireVue says on its candidate resources page that 42% of its interviews are completed outside normal business hours and reports 90% candidate satisfaction, both vendor figures. For a retailer screening thousands of applicants or a hospital hiring night shift staff, letting people interview at midnight on a phone fills the first round in days instead of weeks. The second reason is consistency: every candidate hears the same core questions in the same order, which is harder to guarantee across twenty hiring managers.

The rules that apply in 2026

In New York City, Local Law 144 bars employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless it has had a bias audit within the past year, a summary of the results is public and candidates receive notice; the city's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection enforces it and takes complaints. Our guide to Local Law 144 bias audits explains what an audit contains.

Illinois requires employers that use AI to analyze video interviews to tell applicants, explain how the AI works, get consent and delete the recordings on request; see the Illinois AI Video Interview Act explainer. Colorado's broader law on high risk AI systems covers hiring decisions too, as our Colorado AI Act page sets out, and in the EU recruitment AI is classed as high risk under the EU AI Act.

How to prepare as a candidate

  • Read the invitation for a practice question. Most platforms offer one, and it shows you the timer and retake rules.
  • Have three or four stories ready that show the skills in the job ad, each with a clear result.
  • Use a quiet room and a stable connection; audio quality affects the transcript more than video quality affects anything.
  • Ask the employer, by email, whether a human reviews every interview and how to request an accommodation. Both are reasonable questions.

Rehearsal tools can help with nerves; our AI interview practice explainer compares them. Tools that feed you answers during the live interview are a different matter, and employers increasingly detect them.

How to run one well as an employer

Keep the AI round short, ideally under fifteen minutes, and tell candidates in the invitation what it covers and who reviews it. Configure questions from the job's real competencies rather than a generic library, and audit outcomes by stage: if completion rates fall for one group of applicants, the format is costing you candidates. Always give a route to a human interview for people who need an accommodation, and make sure a recruiter reads the evidence notes before anyone is rejected.

faq.q: What is an AI job interview?
faq.a: It is a first round interview run by software instead of a person. The system asks questions by video, voice or chat, records or transcribes the answers and sends a summary or score to a recruiter.

faq.q: Does the AI watch my facial expressions?
faq.a: In most current products, no. Scoring is based on the transcript of what you say, mapped to the skills the employer chose. Ask the employer if you want confirmation for a specific tool.

faq.q: Can an AI job interview reject me on its own?
faq.a: Some systems can screen candidates out automatically, which is why laws like New York City's Local Law 144 require bias audits and notice. Many employers still have a recruiter review results before any rejection.

faq.q: Can I ask for a human interviewer instead?
faq.a: Yes. You can ask for an accommodation or an alternative format, and employers covered by disability law must consider reasonable requests.

title: AI assessment tools explained: what they test, how the scoring works and the fairness rules that apply
seoTitle: AI Assessment Tools for Hiring: How They Work and What to Check
description: A plain English guide to AI assessment tools in hiring for 2026: game based, simulation, coding and AI scored open response tests, what vendors claim about prediction, the four fifths rule, NYC Local Law 144 and the questions to ask before buying.
short: What AI powered candidate assessments measure, where the AI sits, how to judge validity and the legal checks employers must run.
body:
An AI assessment tool is software that tests job candidates on skills, abilities or work behaviors and uses machine learning to build the test, score the answers or both. That covers a wide range of products in 2026: game based cognitive tasks, simulations of a day on the job, auto scored coding exercises, open text and spoken answers graded by language models, and proctoring that watches for cheating. They are sold to replace or shrink the resume screen, on the argument that what someone can do in twenty minutes predicts performance better than what they wrote about themselves. Whether that argument holds depends on how the tool was built and validated, which is what this explainer is about.

The main types you will see

Game based tasks. Short puzzles and reaction exercises that measure memory, attention, risk taking or problem solving. Harver sells these under the pymetrics name, and HireVue lists games that measure cognitive ability on its assessments page.

Job simulations and situational judgment. The candidate works through realistic scenarios, such as an upset customer or a conflicting set of priorities, and chooses or writes a response. HireVue calls its version a Virtual Job Tryout; SHL sells situational judgment tests alongside its OPQ personality questionnaire and Verify ability tests.

Technical and coding tests. Programming problems scored automatically against test cases, often with the system flagging copied or machine generated code. These are the most direct measures in the category, because the task is close to the work.

Open response scored by AI. Written or spoken answers that a language model grades against a rubric. Criteria sells cognitive aptitude, personality, emotional intelligence and risk tests and offers an AI scoring add on for its video interviews. TestGorilla combines a skills test library with simulations and AI interviews.

Where the AI actually sits

It helps to separate three jobs. First, building the test: some vendors use AI to generate items or adapt difficulty to each candidate. Second, scoring: a model turns answers, choices or response patterns into a number. Third, protecting the test: Criteria, for example, lists AI proctoring among its products, and many vendors now monitor for tabs, second devices and pasted answers because candidates use AI assistants too. A product can use AI for any one of these and still call itself an AI assessment, so ask which.

Does it predict job performance?

Vendors publish striking numbers. HireVue says its assessments draw on more than 200 million completions and that sales candidates who score high are seven times more likely to become top performers than those who score low; those are vendor figures from its own customers. The honest answer for any buyer is that predictive power is local. A test validated for call center agents tells you little about warehouse leads. Ask for a validation study that matches your role, sample size and outcome measure, and check whether the outcome was a supervisor rating, retention or actual output.

Fairness and the legal baseline

In the United States the oldest rule is still the most useful. The federal Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, adopted in 1978, say that a selection rate for any race, sex or ethnic group that is less than four fifths of the rate for the group with the highest rate will generally be regarded as evidence of adverse impact. That applies to an AI assessment exactly as it applies to a paper test, and the employer, not the vendor, carries the risk. Our explainer on AI bias in hiring covers how disparities arise.

Local rules add obligations. New York City's Local Law 144 bars employers from using an automated employment decision tool unless it has had a bias audit within the past year, the results summary is public and candidates get notice; the city's enforcement agency says that notice must come 10 business days before use. See our guide to Local Law 144 bias audits, and the Colorado AI Act page for a state level approach. Disability law also applies: a timed game or a speech scored test can disadvantage some candidates, so offer an accommodation route and say how to request it.

Questions to ask a vendor before you buy

  • Which job analysis links each scored trait to the role you are hiring for?
  • Can we see adverse impact results by group for a comparable role, and will you run them on our own data after launch?
  • Is any score produced by a model we cannot inspect, and can a recruiter see why a candidate scored as they did?
  • What accommodations are built in, such as extra time, screen reader support or a non timed alternative?
  • How long are responses and recordings kept, and can a candidate ask for deletion?

How candidates experience them

Assessments usually arrive soon after the application. Candidates do better when the employer explains what is measured, why it matters for the job and whether a person reviews results before any rejection. Short, job relevant tasks keep completion rates up; long generic batteries drive good applicants away. For the wider shift away from credentials, read skills based hiring and AI.

faq.q: What are AI assessment tools in hiring?
faq.a: They are candidate tests that use machine learning to build questions, score answers or monitor for cheating. Common formats are game based tasks, job simulations, coding tests and written or spoken answers graded by a model.

faq.q: Are AI assessments legal?
faq.a: Yes, but the same anti discrimination rules apply as to any selection test. Employers should check adverse impact using the four fifths rule in the federal Uniform Guidelines, and in New York City an annual bias audit and candidate notice are required.

faq.q: Do AI assessments predict job performance?
faq.a: Some do for specific roles, but the evidence is local. Ask the vendor for a validation study on a role like yours and an outcome you care about, such as performance ratings or retention.

faq.q: Can candidates ask for an accommodation?
faq.a: Yes. Timed or speech based tests can disadvantage people with some disabilities, so employers should offer and explain an accommodation or alternative format.

faq.q: Can candidates use AI to cheat on these tests?
faq.a: Some try, which is why vendors increasingly add proctoring that watches for pasted answers, second devices and tab switching.

title: The EEOC and artificial intelligence in hiring: what still applies after the 2025 rollback
seoTitle: EEOC and AI in Hiring: What Still Applies in 2026
description: What the EEOC enforces when employers use AI to screen candidates in 2026: Title VII, the ADA and the ADEA, the Uniform Guidelines, the removed AI guidance, the April 2025 executive order on disparate impact and the iTutorGroup settlement.
short: Why the EEOC's AI guidance disappeared, which federal laws still cover automated hiring tools and what recruiting teams should check.
body:
Search for the EEOC and artificial intelligence and you will still find checklists that send you to an agency page explaining how Title VII applies to algorithmic hiring tools. Follow the link today and you get a 404. On November 24, 2026 the address eeoc.gov/ai returned the agency's standard page not found screen when we loaded it. That missing page is the most visible sign of a bigger shift: the federal agency that enforces job discrimination law has stopped publishing AI specific advice, while the laws it enforces have not changed at all.

This explainer separates the two. It covers what the EEOC actually enforces, what changed in 2025, the one AI hiring case the agency settled, and what that means for a recruiting team that screens, ranks or interviews candidates with software in 2026.

What the EEOC enforces, with or without AI

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission enforces three statutes that matter most for hiring tools. Its guidance page on employment tests and selection procedures says Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act all prohibit discriminatory tests and selection procedures. None of these laws mentions artificial intelligence, and none needs to. A resume ranking model, a chatbot that asks knockout questions and a scored video interview are all selection procedures in the plain sense of the term.

The same page describes two ways a test can break Title VII:

  • Disparate treatment: intentionally treating applicants differently because of race, color, religion, sex or national origin, for example testing one group and not another.
  • Disparate impact: using a neutral looking procedure that disproportionately excludes a protected group when the procedure is not job related and consistent with business necessity.

Since 1978 employers have measured that second risk with the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, codified at 29 C.F.R. Part 1607, which the EEOC adopted under Title VII. The guidelines are the source of the familiar four fifths comparison of selection rates. The EEOC page also tells employers to look for an equally effective alternative with less adverse impact and to keep checking that a test still predicts performance. Our explainer on AI bias in hiring walks through how that math is run on an automated screen.

What changed in 2025

Two federal moves rewrote the tone, if not the text, of the rules.

DateActionEffect on AI hiring tools
Early 2025EEOC AI technical assistance pages taken downNo current federal document explains how the agency views algorithmic screening
April 23, 2025Executive order Restoring Equality of Opportunity and MeritocracyFederal policy is to eliminate disparate impact liability "to the maximum degree possible"; the Attorney General and the EEOC Chair were told to review pending matters that rely on it
UnchangedTitle VII, ADA, ADEA and 29 C.F.R. Part 1607Still law; private plaintiffs can still sue

Section 6 of the order directed the Attorney General and the EEOC Chair to assess, within 45 days, all pending investigations and civil suits under federal civil rights laws, including Title VII, that rely on a disparate impact theory. An executive order cannot amend a statute, though. Disparate impact under Title VII comes from the text Congress wrote and from Supreme Court precedent, so the practical change is about federal enforcement priorities. A rejected candidate, a class action firm or a state agency can still bring the claim.

The one AI hiring case the EEOC settled

The agency's clearest automated hiring case is not about machine learning at all. In a September 11, 2023 press release, the EEOC announced that iTutorGroup would pay $365,000 to settle a suit alleging its tutor application software was programmed to automatically reject women aged 55 or older and men aged 60 or older. According to the agency, more than 200 qualified applicants in the United States were rejected because of their age, which violates the ADEA. The money went to the applicants who were screened out.

The lesson for 2026 is that the riskiest automation is often a simple rule hidden inside a form, not a neural network. A birth year filter, a graduation date cutoff or a radius rule that tracks a neighborhood's demographics can do the same damage, and they are easier to prove in court. The age theory is also at the center of the collective action against an HR software vendor described in our Mobley v. Workday explainer.

Where the rules are written now

With federal guidance gone, the detailed requirements come from states and cities. New York City's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection still runs its automated employment decision tools page, which lets the public report an employer or employment agency that used a tool without a bias audit, without posting the audit summary or without giving the required notices. The city clarified in June 2023 that the notice must go out 10 business days before the tool is used. The details are in our NYC Local Law 144 guide, and the state picture is covered in the explainers on Colorado and Texas. For a single dated map of which regimes are in force, see this AI hiring compliance timeline.

A working checklist for recruiting teams

  1. Inventory every automated step. List each place software scores, filters, ranks or rejects candidates, including knockout questions in the ATS.
  2. Run selection rate comparisons yourself. The Uniform Guidelines still apply. Compare pass rates by sex, race and ethnicity, and by age bands of 40 and over, at every stage.
  3. Remove proxy rules. Graduation year, years since degree and similar fields can stand in for age.
  4. Ask vendors for validation evidence. A tool that disproportionately screens out a group needs proof that it is job related.
  5. Offer accommodations. The ADA covers timed games, video analysis and chat screens; tell candidates how to request an alternative format.
  6. Keep records. If a charge arrives, you will need the tool version, the criteria and the outcomes for that requisition.

The short version: the EEOC no longer explains how it views AI in hiring, but the statutes it enforces still apply to every automated decision, and plaintiffs and states have more reason than ever to use them.

faq.q: Does the EEOC regulate artificial intelligence in hiring?
faq.a: Not with an AI specific rule. It enforces Title VII, the ADA and the ADEA, and those laws cover any test or selection procedure, including software that screens, ranks or rejects applicants.

faq.q: Is the EEOC's AI guidance still available?
faq.a: No. The agency's AI technical assistance was taken down in early 2025, and eeoc.gov/ai returned a page not found error when we checked on November 24, 2026.

faq.q: Did the 2025 executive order end disparate impact claims?
faq.a: No. It set a federal policy against disparate impact liability and told the Attorney General and the EEOC Chair to review pending matters, but Title VII itself was not amended and private lawsuits remain possible.

faq.q: What was the iTutorGroup case?
faq.a: The EEOC alleged iTutorGroup's application software automatically rejected women 55 and older and men 60 and older. The company agreed in 2023 to pay $365,000 to settle the age discrimination suit.

title: AI recruiters in 2026: the five hiring jobs the software takes over, and where people still decide
seoTitle: AI Recruiter Explained: What It Does at Each Hiring Stage
description: What an AI recruiter actually does in 2026, stage by stage: sourcing, outreach, screening chat, scheduling and AI interviews, with examples from LinkedIn, Paradox, HireVue and Wellfound, the audit and notice rules that apply, and what still needs a human.
short: A stage by stage map of what AI recruiters do in 2026, which products cover which step, and the rules that apply when software screens candidates.
body:
Verdict first: an AI recruiter in 2026 is not one product. It is a label vendors put on software that takes over one or more recruiting steps, usually finding people, starting the conversation, screening answers, booking the interview or running a first round interview itself. Very few tools do all five well, and none of them make the hiring decision on their own in the products we reviewed. If you are buying, map the step you want to hand off before you look at demos. If you are a candidate who has just been contacted by one, the same map tells you what is on the other end of the message.

Five jobs that get called an AI recruiter

StageWhat the software doesExample from a vendor pageWho still decides
SourcingRuns searches, scores profiles against the roleLinkedIn Hiring Assistant 2Recruiter picks who to contact
First contactWrites and sends personalized messagesWellfound AI agents, NoonRecruiter approves the target list and tone
Screening chatAsks knockout questions by chat or textParadox, HireVue chat agentRules set by the employer
SchedulingOffers slots and books interviewsParadox conversational schedulingHiring manager owns the calendar
First interviewRuns a structured interview at any hourHireVue AI InterviewerRecruiter reviews the evidence and shortlists

Sourcing: where most of the hype lives

Sourcing is the step most vendors mean when they say AI recruiter. LinkedIn's Hiring Assistant 2 page describes an agent that runs dozens of searches across the network, draws on signals from more than 1.3 billion members and learns from a recruiter's feedback on each match. LinkedIn claims recruiters find qualified matches while reviewing 83 percent fewer profiles, and are four times as likely to contact a candidate the assistant surfaced than one found through traditional methods. Those are vendor figures, not independent results, but they show what the product is built to do: shrink the list a human reads.

Outside a single network, sourcing agents search the open web, GitHub, publications and company sites. Noon's AI Sourcer, for example, searches beyond LinkedIn, evaluates each profile against the role's criteria and keeps sourcing as new people appear, then hands candidates to personalized email and SMS outreach. Agency recruiters have their own version: Paraform gives independent recruiters free AI sourcing, matching, a CRM, a notetaker and a scheduler, and connects them with open roles from startups and enterprises.

Outreach: the message a candidate actually sees

For candidates, the AI recruiter usually shows up as an email or text. Wellfound says its agents find candidates, write personalized outreach and send it from the employer's own inbox around the clock. That design matters: the message comes from a real person's address, so replies land with a human. The quality test is simple. A good AI written message names something specific from the candidate's background and states pay, location and the role's scope. A bad one could have been sent to anyone, and candidates delete those quickly.

Screening and scheduling: the frontline workhorse

For hourly and frontline hiring, the AI recruiter is a chat or text assistant. Paradox sells a conversational ATS and a Candidate Experience Agent that validate qualifications through chat or text, let candidates pick interview times and send prep material, and it markets an integration that brings two way SMS and automated scheduling to Workday customers. Here the AI is not judging talent so much as removing waiting time: a restaurant applicant who can book an interview at 11 p.m. on a phone does not wander off to the next job post.

AI interviews: the step that draws the most scrutiny

HireVue now markets agentic hiring tools, including a website chat agent that steers applicants toward suitable roles and an AI Interviewer that gives every applicant a 24/7 screening interview, with each recommendation accompanied by the evidence behind it. HireVue says 40 percent of the Fortune 100 use its platform. This is also where law reaches first. New York City's AEDT rules bar employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless it has had a bias audit within the past year, a summary of the audit is public and candidates receive the required notices. In California, the privacy agency's board adopted regulations on automated decisionmaking technology on July 24, 2025. Our explainers on Local Law 144 and the Colorado AI Act cover the details.

What an AI recruiter still cannot do

None of these tools close a hire. They do not sell a reluctant passive candidate on a move across the country, negotiate a counteroffer or read a hiring manager's unspoken preferences. They also inherit whatever is wrong with the job description and the criteria they are given. A team that has not agreed on what good looks like will get a very fast stream of the wrong people.

Three questions separate useful products from marketing. Which step does it fully own, and where does a human sign off? What does it record about why a candidate was ranked or rejected, and can you export that record for an audit? And when it contacts a candidate, whose name is on the message and who answers the reply?

If an AI recruiter contacts you

Treat it like any recruiter message. Check that the company and role are real, answer the specific questions it asks and expect a human at the interview stage. In New York City you are entitled to a notice when an automated tool is used to screen you. Anywhere, you can ask the recruiter whether AI was used to rank your application and what a person reviewed.

faq.q: What is an AI recruiter?
faq.a: Software that takes over one or more recruiting steps: sourcing candidates, writing first messages, screening by chat or text, scheduling interviews or running a first round interview. A human still makes the hiring decision.

faq.q: Will an AI recruiter replace human recruiters?
faq.a: Not in the products reviewed here. They cut the time spent searching, messaging and scheduling, but people still decide who advances, negotiate offers and close hires.

faq.q: Is it legal to use an AI recruiter to screen candidates?
faq.a: Yes, with conditions. New York City requires a bias audit within the past year, a public audit summary and candidate notices before an automated employment decision tool is used, and federal anti discrimination law applies to any screening method.

faq.q: How can I tell if an AI recruiter contacted me?
faq.a: Generic wording, instant replies at odd hours and fixed menu style questions are common signs. You can simply ask whether the message or screening was automated and who will review your answers.

faq.q: What does LinkedIn's Hiring Assistant do?
faq.a: LinkedIn says Hiring Assistant 2 runs dozens of searches across LinkedIn, learns from recruiter feedback and lets recruiters find qualified matches while reviewing 83 percent fewer profiles.

faq.q: Which AI recruiter is best for hourly hiring?
faq.a: Conversational tools like Paradox are designed for frontline roles, with screening by text, self scheduling and mobile first applications.

title: AI job applications in 2026: auto apply tools, the employer backlash and what still gets read
seoTitle: AI Job Applications Explained: Auto Apply Tools and Employer Response
description: What an AI job application is in 2026, from resume tailoring to auto apply bots like LazyApply and JobCopilot, how employers are changing screening in response, and what Greenhouse's 2026 employer and candidate surveys found.
short: Four levels of AI help on a job application, what auto apply tools claim, and how employers changed screening in 2026.
body:
What happens when a job seeker lets software apply for them? In 2026 the honest answer is: the application goes out faster, the employer trusts it less, and a human on the hiring side ends up doing more work to tell real candidates from noise. An AI job application is any application where a candidate used AI to find the role, rewrite the resume or cover letter, answer screening questions or submit the form itself. The last case, automated submission at volume, is the one that has changed how employers screen.

Four levels of AI help on an application

LevelWhat the AI doesWho presses submitHow employers tend to see it
Writing helpEdits a resume or drafts a cover letterThe candidateNormal, if the claims are true
TailoringRewrites the resume for each posting's keywordsThe candidateFine until skills are added that the person lacks
Assisted applyFills forms and answers screening questionsThe candidate, after reviewHard to detect, mixed reception
Auto applyFinds jobs and submits applications on a scheduleThe softwareThe main source of the volume complaint

What auto apply tools say they do

Vendor pages describe the category plainly. LazyApply says its Job GPT applies on Greenhouse, Dice, Indeed and ZipRecruiter and sells annual plans of $99 for 15 applications a day and $149 for 150 a day. JobCopilot says it applies to up to 50 personalized applications a day from more than 500,000 companies. AIApply bundles job search, resume and cover letter tailoring, auto apply and live interview coaching. The pitch is the same everywhere: the average applicant sends dozens of applications per interview, so send more of them.

The math works for one candidate and breaks for the market. If every applicant sends ten times as many applications, each employer reads ten times as many, and the share that gets a conversation falls. Greenhouse's Fall 2026 Hire Standard report, quoted in its November 19, 2026 release, says 97% of applications never reach a conversation.

How employers are reacting

The same Greenhouse employer report surveyed 1,347 US recruiters and hiring managers. Nine in ten (90%) believe they have turned away real candidates because the application looked fake or AI generated. 86% changed their hiring process because of fake or AI generated applications, and of those, 57% added another human interview. 81% have seen applicants try new ways to get past screening, including claiming skills they do not have (49%) and hiding text in resumes aimed at AI reviewers (28%).

Two responses are spreading. The first is earlier live contact: 54% of employers said they would consider a live conversation or interview earlier, and 52% already use AI interviews, which lets a team hear from more applicants than recruiters could phone screen. The second is identity and fraud checks; see our explainer on deepfake job candidates for where that ends. On the screening side, employers increasingly rely on applicant screening software that scores every inbound application against the role rather than keyword filters that tailored resumes are written to beat.

What candidates report

Greenhouse's 2026 candidate report of more than 2,800 US job seekers shows the other side. 77% used AI in their search in the past year, and 81% were rejected without a single conversation. 62% tried tactics to get past automated screening, such as using AI to work out what the system looks for (54%) or adding skills and keywords they do not have (40%). At the same time, 39% rewrote an application so it would not be mistaken for AI, and another 21% considered it.

So the arms race runs both ways: candidates use AI to get past filters, then edit their writing so it does not read as AI. Our pages on AI generated resumes and how ATS screening reads a resume cover the document side in more detail.

Rules and terms that apply

The limits candidates run into are mostly contractual and practical. Job sites set terms for automated access: LinkedIn's User Agreement, for example, prohibits using bots or other unauthorized automated methods to access its services or send messages. And an employer can reject an application that contains false statements no matter who typed them. On the employer side, if your screening software ranks or rejects applicants, the bias audit and notice rules in our NYC Local Law 144 explainer and the federal picture in EEOC and AI in hiring still apply, even when the applications themselves were machine written.

Practical advice for both sides

Employers: add one short, role specific question that a bot cannot answer from the posting, move a live conversation earlier for shortlisted applicants, and tell candidates when a human will review their answers. In the Greenhouse candidate survey, 49% wanted to know a human would review their responses.

It also helps to be clear about what you will not automate. When Greenhouse asked employers which tasks they would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates advance came last, at 7%. Saying so in the job post, along with what the first conversation will cover, gives careful applicants a reason to apply once rather than through a bot. 85% of employers in the same survey said they want applications to reveal more about candidates, which is an argument for asking fewer, better questions instead of longer forms.

Candidates: use AI to draft and tailor, but apply to fewer roles you actually fit, remove any skill you cannot demonstrate in an interview, and expect the employer to test claims early.

faq.q: What is an AI job application?
faq.a: Any application where a candidate used AI to find the job, tailor the resume or cover letter, answer screening questions or submit the form. Auto apply tools go furthest and submit applications for the candidate on a schedule.

faq.q: Do employers reject AI written applications?
faq.a: Not automatically, but trust has dropped. In Greenhouse's 2026 employer survey, 90% believed they had turned away real candidates because applications seemed fake or AI generated, and 86% had changed their hiring process in response.

faq.q: How many applications do auto apply tools send?
faq.a: Vendor pages list limits such as 15 or 150 applications a day on LazyApply's annual plans and up to 50 a day on JobCopilot.

faq.q: Is using an auto apply tool against the rules?
faq.a: It depends on the job site. Many restrict automated access in their terms, LinkedIn among them, and any false claim on an application can still lead to rejection or a rescinded offer.

title: AI cover letters in 2026: how the generators work, why they read alike and what recruiters look for now
seoTitle: AI Cover Letters Explained: Generators, Detection and Recruiters
description: What an AI cover letter is, how generators like Kickresume and ResumeBuilder.com build one from a resume and job post, why OpenAI withdrew its AI text detector, and how recruiters now read letters.
short: How AI cover letter generators work, why detectors fail, and what recruiters look for once every letter is fluent.
body:
26 percent. That was the share of AI written text OpenAI's own detector correctly flagged in its evaluation, while it wrongly labeled human writing as AI 9 percent of the time. OpenAI withdrew that classifier on July 20, 2023, citing its low rate of accuracy. Keep those two numbers in mind whenever someone claims a hiring team can reliably spot an AI cover letter. The useful questions in 2026 are different: what AI cover letter tools actually do, why so many letters now read alike, and how recruiters adjust.

What an AI cover letter is

An AI cover letter is a letter drafted wholly or partly by a language model from the job posting and the candidate's resume. Dedicated generators sit inside resume builders: Kickresume markets a GPT-4.1 powered cover letter writer, and ResumeBuilder.com offers a generator that tailors a letter to the resume and target role. Many candidates skip those and paste the posting into a general chat assistant. Either way, the output is a fluent, well structured letter in under a minute, which is exactly why it no longer stands out.

How the generators work

Most tools follow the same three steps. They read the job description and pull out required skills and keywords. They read the resume and pick the experiences that match. Then they fill a familiar template: an opening that names the role, two paragraphs linking past work to the posting, and a closing that asks for an interview. Tone sliders and length settings change the surface, not the structure. The model has no knowledge of the candidate beyond what it was given, so anything specific about the company or the person has to come from the user.

Part of the letterWhat AI handles wellWhere it usually goes wrong
OpeningNames the role and company correctlyGeneric enthusiasm that could fit any employer
Matching skillsMirrors keywords from the postingClaims skills the resume does not support
EvidenceRestates resume bullets in proseInflates numbers or invents results
Company knowledgeRepeats the mission statementGets products, locations or recent news wrong
ClosingPolite, correct call to actionIdentical phrasing across thousands of letters

What changes for recruiters

When every letter is fluent, fluency stops being a signal. Recruiters who still read letters tend to look for the things a model cannot invent from a posting: a specific reason for wanting this employer, a concrete result with context, or a connection to someone at the company. Many teams have quietly made the letter optional and moved the same questions into short screening prompts on the application, which are harder to answer generically. Our explainer on AI generated resumes covers the same shift for the resume itself, and AI job applications covers the auto apply tools that send letters at scale.

Why detection is a weak policy

The OpenAI figures above are the cleanest public evidence that detectors miss most AI text while still accusing some humans. Rejecting candidates on a detector score risks screening out people who simply write in a plain, organized style, including many non native English speakers. A better policy is to judge the letter on accuracy and specificity, and to verify claims in the interview the same way you would for any candidate. If an ATS or screening tool scores letters, ask the vendor what it measures; our guide to AI resume parsing explains what those systems can and cannot read.

Using AI for a cover letter without hurting your chances

For candidates, the practical rule is to let the tool draft and then replace its weakest sentences with facts only you know. Check every claim against your resume. Cut the opening line if it would fit any job. Add one sentence about why this company, with a detail from its own site or a conversation. Read it aloud once; letters that sound like a press release usually came straight out of a generator. Employers writing their own postings with AI face the mirror image of this problem, covered in AI job description generators.

Should employers still ask for a cover letter?

It depends on what the letter is for. If the job involves writing to clients, drafting reports or explaining decisions, a letter is still a fair work sample, but only if you ask for something a generator cannot fake: a short answer about a real problem your team has, or a response to a scenario in the posting. If the letter is a ritual nobody reads, drop it. Making it optional and saying so in the posting is more honest than requiring a document that every applicant now produces in seconds, and it shortens the application for the people you most want to finish it.

Whatever you choose, be consistent. Evaluating some letters for effort and ignoring others introduces exactly the kind of uneven screening that hiring audits look for, and a written rule is easy to explain to candidates who ask.

A five point check for any letter, written by a person or a model

Recruiters who still read letters can use the same short test regardless of who or what drafted it. First, does it name a reason for this employer that would not fit a competitor? Second, does every claim match the resume? Third, is there at least one result with a number and a context? Fourth, does the closing ask for something specific, such as a conversation about a named project? Fifth, would you remember it an hour later? A letter that passes three or more is doing its job, whatever tool helped write it.

faq.q: Can recruiters tell if a cover letter was written by AI?
faq.a: Not reliably. OpenAI's own classifier caught 26 percent of AI written text and flagged 9 percent of human text as AI before OpenAI withdrew it in July 2023. Recruiters notice generic letters, not AI as such.

faq.q: Is it acceptable to use AI to write a cover letter?
faq.a: Most employers do not ban it. What hurts a candidate is inaccurate claims or a letter that could fit any company, so edit the draft with specific facts.

faq.q: Do employers still read cover letters in 2026?
faq.a: Some do, especially for writing heavy and senior roles, but many have made them optional and use short screening questions on the application instead.

title: AI interview questions: how to test whether a candidate can actually work with AI
seoTitle: AI Interview Questions: 8 That Test Real AI Fluency
description: AI interview questions explained for 2026: what TestGorilla's survey of 2,000 hiring leaders found, eight questions built on the 4D AI Fluency Framework, a ten minute output review and a scoring scale.
short: Eight questions and a short exercise that separate people who use AI well from people who only talk about it.
body:
Fifty nine percent. That is the share of organizations in TestGorilla's State of Hiring for AI Fluency 2026 survey of about 2,000 senior hiring leaders in the US and UK that say they have already made a bad AI hire: someone who named the right tools in the interview and could not use them on the job. The same report found that 95% list AI fluency as a hiring requirement and 71% have formally defined it. The gap is not intent. It is the questions. This explainer covers what people mean by AI interview questions, which questions actually separate practitioners from talkers, and how to score the answers fairly.

Two things people mean by AI interview questions

The phrase is used in two ways. Most hiring managers mean questions that test whether a candidate can work well with AI tools, now a requirement in roles from marketing to finance. A smaller group means the questions an automated interviewer asks candidates during a screening call. This page focuses on the first meaning, with a short section on the second. For the software that runs automated screens, see our explainer on AI interviewers.

Why ordinary questions miss

Asking "How do you use AI?" invites a tour of tool names. TestGorilla's report describes the core problem as an interview that rewards the best storyteller rather than the best operator: it observes communication, not execution. It also found that 19% of organizations leave AI assessment entirely to each hiring manager's judgment, with no shared rubric. Two candidates with equal skill can get opposite verdicts depending on which manager they meet. Better questions ask for a specific past task, the checking step and a decision not to use AI.

A question bank built on the 4D framework

A practical structure comes from the AI Fluency Framework by Rick Dakan, Joseph Feller and Anthropic, which splits fluency into four competencies: delegation, description, discernment and diligence. Each maps to questions an interviewer can probe.

CompetencyQuestion to askA strong answer includesA weak answer sounds like
DelegationTell me about a task you decided not to hand to AI. Why?A concrete risk, such as confidential data or judgment the model lacks"I use it for everything"
DelegationWhich part of your current job would you automate first, and what would you keep?A clear split between repeatable steps and decisionsA list of tools with no workflow
DescriptionShow me a prompt that failed and how you changed it.The original instruction, what went wrong and the specific fixGeneric tips about being specific
DescriptionHow would you brief an AI tool on our brand voice or data format?Examples, constraints and a format for the output"I would just ask it"
DiscernmentDescribe a time AI output was confidently wrong. How did you catch it?A verification step against a source or testNo example, or "it is usually right"
DiscernmentHow do you check a number or citation an assistant gives you?Going to the primary source before using itTrusting the link without opening it
DiligenceWhen do you tell a manager or client that AI helped with a piece of work?A rule they follow and a reason for itNever thought about it
DiligenceWhat would you never paste into a public AI tool?Personal data, client files, unreleased financialsUnsure, or nothing

Ask two or three, not all eight, and follow each with "What happened next?" until the candidate either gives detail or runs out of story.

Add a ten minute output review

The fastest way past rehearsed answers is a short exercise every candidate can do, whatever tools their last employer allowed. Hand over a one page AI generated draft relevant to the role, such as a customer email, a summary of a spreadsheet or a code snippet, with three planted problems: a wrong figure, an invented source and a tone mismatch. Give ten minutes to mark it up. Candidates who find all three and explain how they would fix the prompt are showing discernment you cannot fake in conversation.

Score answers on a written scale

Write anchors before the first interview. A simple four point scale works: 1 for no example, 2 for a real example without a check, 3 for a real example with a verification step, 4 for an example where the candidate also changed their process afterward. Score each competency separately, compare notes only after everyone has scored, and keep the same questions for every candidate in the same role. That structure answers the subjectivity problem TestGorilla describes and makes decisions easier to defend if a candidate challenges them.

Questions an AI interviewer asks you

When the interviewer is software, the questions are usually set by the employer in advance and are often the same structured screening questions a recruiter would ask: availability, work authorization, experience with specific tasks and a few behavioral prompts. The system records and transcribes answers and may score them against the employer's criteria. In Illinois, New York City and Colorado, specific notice or audit rules apply, covered in our explainer on AI job interviews. Candidates should answer as they would to a person: concrete examples, short and in order.

Keep it fair

Questions about AI use should be tied to the job. A warehouse supervisor does not need to write prompts, and asking about it adds noise. Avoid penalizing candidates whose past employer banned AI tools; the output review exercise is the fix for that, because it tests judgment rather than habit. And separate this topic from catching candidates who use AI to answer interview questions in real time, which is a different policy question covered in our explainer on AI interview assistants.

faq.q: What are good interview questions about AI?
faq.a: Questions that ask for a specific past task: a prompt that failed and how it was fixed, a time AI output was wrong and how it was caught, and a task the candidate chose not to give to AI.

faq.q: How do you assess AI skills in an interview?
faq.a: Combine two or three structured questions with a short output review exercise, and score each answer against anchors written before the interview.

faq.q: What is AI fluency?
faq.a: The AI Fluency Framework by Rick Dakan, Joseph Feller and Anthropic defines it as working with AI effectively, efficiently, ethically and safely, across four competencies: delegation, description, discernment and diligence.

faq.q: How many companies require AI fluency when hiring?
faq.a: In TestGorilla's 2026 survey of about 2,000 US and UK hiring leaders, 95% listed AI fluency as a requirement and 71% had formally defined it.

faq.q: Do AI interviewers ask different questions from humans?
faq.a: Usually not. Employers set the questions, which tend to be structured screening and behavioral questions; the software records, transcribes and may score the answers.

faq.q: Should I ask AI questions for every role?
faq.a: Only where the job uses AI tools. For roles that do not, the questions add noise and can disadvantage strong candidates.

title: AI personality tests in hiring: what they measure, where the AI sits and what to ask a vendor
seoTitle: AI Personality Tests for Hiring: How They Work
description: A plain English explainer of AI personality tests used in hiring in 2026: questionnaire based tools like Hogan and Harver, game and image formats like Traitify, profile inference tools like Crystal, and the legal questions employers face.
short: Three kinds of tool share the label, and only one of them asks the candidate anything.
body:
Picture two candidates for the same customer success job. One spends twelve minutes answering a questionnaire about how she handles deadlines and conflict. The other never takes a test at all, yet the recruiter's browser extension shows a confident personality label next to his public profile. Both results get called an AI personality test. They are very different things, and the difference decides how much weight either result deserves in a hiring decision.

Three tools behind one label

When vendors and job seekers say AI personality test, they usually mean one of three things.

TypeWhat the candidate doesWhere AI is usedExample
Scored questionnaireAnswers statements about their own behaviorScoring, norming against role data, report writingHogan Personality Inventory, Harver Personality Questionnaire
Visual or game formatReacts to images or short tasks on a phoneMapping quick choices to trait scoresTraitify, now part of Paradox
Inference from textNothing; the tool reads profiles, emails or writing samplesPredicting traits from languageCrystal

The first two still ask the person to respond, so the result reflects something the candidate chose to tell you. The third infers personality without the candidate taking part, which is useful for tailoring a sales conversation and much harder to defend as a selection tool.

What they actually measure

Most hiring tools are built on the Big Five model: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and emotional stability. Traitify described its image based assessment as Big Five research delivered in a few minutes on mobile. Hogan separates what it calls the bright side of personality, how people behave at their best, measured by the HPI, from derailers that show up under stress. Harver positions its questionnaire as a way to understand how candidates approach work during pre selection.

Personality scores describe tendencies, not skills. A high conscientiousness score suggests a person tends to be organized; it does not show they can reconcile an account or close a ticket. That is why industrial psychologists recommend combining personality measures with job samples, structured interviews or cognitive tests rather than using them alone. Our explainer on AI assessment tools covers those other formats.

Where the AI adds something

The questionnaire itself is decades old. What AI changes is the work around it: adaptive question order that shortens the test, scoring models trained on the traits of people who succeeded in a specific role, auto generated reports for hiring managers, and natural language summaries of results. Each of those can be checked. Ask the vendor what outcome the model was trained to predict, how many employees were in the training data, and whether the role you are hiring for resembles theirs.

Inference tools rely more heavily on AI because there are no answers to score. Crystal says its own study found 93.3% of 22,902 peer ratings judged its results accurate, a measure of whether colleagues agree with the label, not of whether the label predicts job performance.

The legal questions employers face

Using an automated tool to score candidates can bring it under hiring rules. New York City's Automated Employment Decision Tools law requires a bias audit and candidate notice when such a tool substantially assists a hiring decision; see our explainer on Local Law 144 bias audits. In the European Union, the AI Act treats AI used to evaluate candidates as high risk and prohibits emotion recognition in the workplace, which rules out tools that claim to read personality from facial expressions; our EU AI Act explainer has the details. In the US, employers also remain responsible under federal anti discrimination law and the ADA if a test screens out people with a disability or a protected group at a higher rate, which our page on AI bias in hiring discusses.

Five questions to ask before you buy

  1. Does the candidate answer questions, or does the tool infer traits without their involvement?
  2. What job outcome was the scoring model validated against, and can we see the technical report?
  3. What adverse impact results do you have by sex and race or ethnicity, and how recent are they?
  4. What accommodations are offered for candidates who cannot complete a timed or visual format?
  5. Do candidates receive their own results?

Vendors that answer all five in writing are usually the ones whose scores hold up.

If you are the candidate

Answer consistently and honestly. Most questionnaires include items that detect a pattern of answering to look ideal, and inconsistent answers lower confidence in the result more than an unremarkable profile does. If the format is hard to use because of a disability, ask the employer for an accommodation before you start.

faq.q: What is an AI personality test?
faq.a: A personality assessment in which AI scores the answers, adapts the questions, or infers traits from text instead of asking the candidate. Most hiring tools use the Big Five traits.

faq.q: Are AI personality tests accurate?
faq.a: Questionnaire based tools can predict some job outcomes when validated for the role. Tools that infer personality from public profiles have far less evidence for hiring use.

faq.q: Can employers use personality tests in hiring?
faq.a: Yes, in most places, but automated scoring can trigger bias audit and notice rules in New York City and high risk obligations under the EU AI Act, and employers stay liable for discriminatory effects.

faq.q: Which personality tests do employers use?
faq.a: Common examples include the Hogan Personality Inventory, Harver's Personality Questionnaire and Traitify's image based assessment, now part of Paradox.

faq.q: Can I prepare for an AI personality test?
faq.a: There are no right answers to study. Answer consistently, think about your behavior at work rather than at home, and ask for an accommodation if the format is a barrier.

title: AI job search in 2026: matching, ghost job filters, assistant connectors and the scams to avoid
seoTitle: AI Job Search Explained: Tools, Risks and Tips
description: A plain English explainer of AI job search in 2026: how job board matching, ghost job risk labels like Enhancv's Job Search and assistant connectors work, what the BBB found about employment scams, and how employers are responding.
short: The new tools mostly help you decide which postings to skip.
body:
Forty seven percent. That is the share of U.S. job seekers who told Enhancv's 2026 ghost jobs study they had applied to a role that, it later turned out, never existed. It explains why the newest AI job search tools are less about finding more listings and more about deciding which listings deserve an evening of your time. This explainer covers what AI job search means in late 2026, which tools do what, where the risks are, and what changes on the recruiter's side when candidates search this way.

What AI job search means

AI job search is the use of machine learning or large language models at the start of a job hunt: describing the work you want in plain language instead of keywords, getting ranked matches, being warned about suspicious postings, and having an assistant track what you applied to. It is a separate step from writing the application itself, which our explainer on AI job applications covers, including auto apply bots.

The four kinds of tool

  • Matching inside job boards. Large boards have used algorithms to recommend jobs for years. In a January 2026 interview published by OpenAI, Indeed's chief revenue officer said the company has more than a hundred AI powered features across job search and hiring and had launched Career Scout, an agent that acts like a career coach for job seekers. In China, BOSS Zhipin operator Kanzhun told investors on November 25, 2026 that AI had improved its matching accuracy as monthly users reached 73.0 million (Kanzhun results).
  • Posting risk filters. On November 24, 2026 Enhancv launched Job Search, a board that runs 25 checks on each of 7.5 million postings every hour and labels each one Low, Moderate or High ghost risk (Enhancv announcement). The idea is simple: a posting that has been reposted for months, has no named team, or never shows up on the employer's own careers page is less likely to lead to an interview.
  • Assistant connectors.
